For how the probe distribution becomes truncation lengths and an ASV length window, see amplicon length and truncation. For the whole amplicon path end to end, see the amplicon overview.

docs.title: 16S rRNA (bacteria and archaea)
docs.text:
16S is the default marker: config/config.yaml ships with amplicon.type: 16S.

Where 16S settings come from

The YAML blocks on this page are examples of what to put in your own config; the page itself sets nothing. Two files decide how a 16S run behaves, and they do not overlap:

  • workflow/markers/16S.yaml — the marker pack. Facts about the marker: which databases to use, that the amplicon length is measured by in-silico PCR against SILVA, that Metaxa2 is the region extractor, which ranks the tables have (eight slots on SILVA 144, Domain to Species; seven on SILVA 138.2, which has no kingdom; the last slot, Species, only the separate species database can fill). It holds no run settings, and you normally do not edit it.
  • config/config.yaml, plus any run config merged on top — the choices about your experiment: primers, expected length, truncation, taxon filter, paths.

The pack is read separately and is never merged into the config, so almost no setting can come from both. The exceptions sit under references:. A database path there wins over the pack default — that is how you point at a shared copy of SILVA instead of downloading your own — and references.silva.release replaces the pack's default SILVA release. The full picture is in which file a setting actually comes from.

docs.title: Setting up a run
docs.text:
Set type: 16S and supply the forward and reverse primer FASTAs for the region amplified. The rest of the block below reproduces the shipped defaults for the keys you are most likely to want to set on a 16S run — not every key the run touches; cutadapt, trunc_len and length_filter are covered further down and in the configuration reference. You do not need to copy any of it into your own config to get these values, since the template already provides them. The two exceptions are keep and discard: those ship commented out, so the values shown are the recommended 16S starting point rather than something already in effect.

amplicon:
  type: 16S

  primers:
    fwd: /path/to/fwd_primer.fasta
    rev: /path/to/rev_primer.fasta
    orientation: fixed            # fixed | mixed

  expected_length: auto           # in-silico PCR against SILVA
  probe_length_stat:
    16S: p95                      # which statistic of the probe distribution to use
  min_overlap: 12                 # bp of R1/R2 overlap the truncLen pair must preserve

  extraction:
    enabled: true                 # Metaxa2

  taxonomy:
    method: sintax                # rdp | sintax
    min_boot: 80                  # rdp only
    sintax_cutoff: 0.8            # sintax only
    try_rc: true                  # rdp only
    silva_other: verbatim         # SILVA 144 only: verbatim | strip
    filter:
      enabled: true
      keep:    [d__Bacteria, d__Archaea]          # recommended, ships commented out
      discard: [o__Chloroplast, f__Mitochondria]  # recommended, ships commented out
      discard_min_support: 50                     # best-hit check for discard; null = off
      organelles: metaxa2                         # drop what Metaxa2 calls organelles; off = keep

Note

amplicon.probe_length_stat.16S must be present for a 16S run, whether or not expected_length is auto — MetaFlux checks the key at start-up and exits with a message naming it if it is missing. The shipped config/config.yaml already has it.

docs.title: Reference databases
docs.text: 16S is classified against SILVA. MetaFlux ships two SILVA releases: SILVA 144, the default, and the previous release, SILVA 138.2, which a run can still choose. None of the files needs to be listed in the config: the marker pack carries the file names, download URLs and md5 checksums, and MetaFlux fetches what the run needs on first use into references.refdb_root (default refdb), where it stays cached for later runs. Every download is checked against its md5 before anything uses it; on a mismatch the file is deleted and the run stops.

docs.title: SILVA 144 (default)
docs.text:
The DADA2 files for SILVA 144 are built and published by the SILVA team itself (arb-silva.de); the 138.2 files come from the DADA2 author's own Zenodo record (below). MetaFlux downloads the 144 files from the release folder, release_144, rather than from "current-release", so the address does not change when SILVA 145 comes out.

Pack symbol Path under refdb_root What it is How it arrives silva_train_raw silva/silva_nr99_v144_toGenus_trainset.fa.gz the training set exactly as SILVA publishes it, seven ranks; also the in-silico PCR substrate download from SILVA (rule fetch_silva_train_raw) silva_train silva/silva_nr99_v144_toGenus_7rank_other-verbatim_trainset.fa.gz the same sequences and the same seven ranks, with the kingdom names written without SILVA's --other suffix: RDP training set built locally (rule convert_silva_train) silva_sintax silva/silva_nr99_v144_7rank_other-verbatim_sintax.fa.gz SINTAX database for VSEARCH built locally from silva_train (rule convert_silva_sintax) silva_species silva/silva_v144_assignSpecies.fa.gz addSpecies reference (16S, rdp only) download from SILVA (rule fetch_silva_species)

With amplicon.taxonomy.silva_other: strip (see below) the two built files carry other-stripped instead of other-verbatim in their names, so the two settings never share a cached file. "7rank" in the names says that the files keep all seven SILVA ranks.

The headers look like this — the differences matter for what each step can return:

silva_train_raw  >Bacteria;Pseudomonadati--other;Bacteroidota;Bacteroidia;Bacteroidales;Odoribacteraceae;Odoribacter;
silva_train      >Bacteria;Pseudomonadati;Bacteroidota;Bacteroidia;Bacteroidales;Odoribacteraceae;Odoribacter;
silva_sintax     >25;tax=d:Bacteria,k:Pseudomonadati,p:Bacteroidota,c:Bacteroidia,o:Bacteroidales,f:Odoribacteraceae,g:Odoribacter
silva_species    >AM889137.2051270.2052798 Neisseria meningitidis

The training set is a toGenus release: its lineages stop at genus, with no rank prefixes and no species field. That single fact explains both the addSpecies step and the rank depth of the two taxonomy methods, below.

docs.title: Domain and kingdom
docs.text:
SILVA 144 re-annotated all prokaryote sequences, using LPSN as the main source of names, and added a Kingdom rank between Domain and Phylum. Its lineages therefore have seven ranks where 138.2 had six, and MetaFlux classifies on all seven: on SILVA 144 the domain is written d__ and the kingdom k__, followed by p__ to g__ and, from addSpecies, s__.

d__Bacteria;k__Pseudomonadati;p__Pseudomonadota;c__Gammaproteobacteria;o__Pseudomonadales;f__Pseudomonadaceae;g__Pseudomonas
  • Both come from the classifier, with the same cutoff as every other rank (min_boot under rdp, sintax_cutoff under sintax). The lineage stops at the first rank below the cutoff, so an ASV that the classifier can place in a kingdom but not in a phylum reads, for example, d__Bacteria;k__Bacillati.
  • Nine kingdom names can occur: Pseudomonadati, Bacillati, Fusobacteriati and Thermotogati for Bacteria; Methanobacteriati, Thermoproteati, Nanobdellati and Promethearchaeati for Archaea; and Incertae Sedis, SILVA's placeholder for the few phyla it places in no named kingdom. The few eukaryote outgroup records of the file carry a domain only.
  • The kingdom never carries --other. SILVA files whole phyla under Pseudomonadati--other (all of Bacteroidota, for example) and under Methanobacteriati--other. That is a note about where they sit in SILVA's tree (see the --other suffix, below); at kingdom level it only splits one kingdom into two labels, and the taxon filter reads X--other as X anyway. So rule convert_silva_train writes every kingdom without the suffix, whichever silva_other is set. It rewrites the headers only, never the sequences, and it refuses a file that does not have the shape of a SILVA 144 toGenus file (a 138.2 file, a toSpecies file, a broken download) rather than guess.
  • The rank set is checked. Before any classification, the reference check makes sure that the file the classifier reads has exactly SILVA 144's seven ranks, with a kingdom name in the second one. A SILVA 138.2 file, whose phyla would land in the Kingdom column, or SILVA's own download with its --other kingdoms, stops the run there.

docs.title: The --other suffix (amplicon.taxonomy.silva_other)
docs.text:
SILVA 144 writes X--other for a clade that does not contain the nomenclatural type of taxon X, but whose sequences SILVA still considers part of X — for example Bacillaceae--other next to Bacillaceae, or Bradyrhizobium--other next to Bradyrhizobium. About 40% of the reference sequences carry it somewhere in their lineage. One setting decides what MetaFlux does with it:

silva_other Effect verbatim (default) Names are kept exactly as SILVA writes them, apart from the kingdom, which is always written without the suffix (above). The keep/discard filter treats X--other as X (so g__Bradyrhizobium also removes g__Bradyrhizobium--other), and so does the genus check of addSpecies; the species is written with the plain genus (g__Lactobacillus--other;s__Lactobacillus iners). strip The suffix is removed from every name before the classifier is trained, so X and X--other become one taxon.

On the 16S test set (PRJNA305879, SILVA 144, expected_length: 384, 229 ASVs), the two settings gave the same lineages apart from the suffix itself and the depth some of them reached. Under sintax, strip took 7 ASVs one rank further, 4 of them to genus (124 ASVs with a genus, against 120). Under rdp it took 19 ASVs one rank further and 3 one rank less far, a net 3 more with a genus (104 against 101). Most changes add a rank, because the classifier no longer has to choose between two labels for one taxon.

SILVA 144 also merges a few intermixed taxa into one label joined by +, each part with its own suffix: Enterobacter--other+Klebsiella--other, Rubrivivax--other+Ideonella--other (about 0.2% of the reference sequences). MetaFlux keeps these labels as they are: neither the filter nor addSpecies splits them, so a token g__Klebsiella does not remove an ASV labelled g__Enterobacter--other+Klebsiella--other. Add the full label as a token if you need to.

docs.title: Choosing SILVA 138.2
docs.text:
To run on the previous release, add this to the run config:

references:
  silva:
    release: "138.2"

The 138.2 files are Benjamin Callahan's DADA2 build (Zenodo 14169026): six ranks, Domain to Genus, with no kingdom and no --other suffix. The training set is used as downloaded, with no conversion step, and silva_other has no effect. The tables then have seven slots, d__ Domain, p__ Phylum … s__ Species, and no k__:

d__Bacteria;p__Pseudomonadota;c__Gammaproteobacteria;o__Pseudomonadales;f__Pseudomonadaceae;g__Pseudomonas

The 138.2 files keep their own file names, so switching back and forth never overwrites the other release's files:

Pack symbol Path under refdb_root How it arrives silva_train silva/silva_nr99_v138.2_toGenus_trainset.fa.gz download from Zenodo silva_species silva/silva_v138.2_assignSpecies.fa.gz download from Zenodo silva_sintax silva/silva_nr99_v138.2_sintax.fa.gz built locally from silva_train

docs.title: Using a shared copy
docs.text:
Apart from the release, an entry under references: in the run config is needed only to relocate a file that already exists elsewhere, for instance on a shared filesystem. Under SILVA 144, relocate the files that belong together, so the training set and its SINTAX build always come from the same conversion:

references:
  refdb_root: refdb
  silva:
    train_raw:   /shared/dbs/silva_nr99_v144_toGenus_trainset.fa.gz
    train:       /shared/dbs/silva_nr99_v144_toGenus_7rank_other-verbatim_trainset.fa.gz
    sintax:      /shared/dbs/silva_nr99_v144_7rank_other-verbatim_sintax.fa.gz
    species:     /shared/dbs/silva_v144_assignSpecies.fa.gz

train and sintax are files MetaFlux builds itself, so a path given for them is where MetaFlux writes them, and it rebuilds them there whenever their input or the conversion script is newer (see reference files MetaFlux builds itself).

docs.title: Amplicon length probe (probe_mode: pcr)
docs.text:
SILVA sequences are whole 16S genes (the SILVA 144 files are trimmed to the gene itself, 138.2 still carries some flanking sequence), so the length of the amplicon the primers actually produce has to be worked out rather than read off the database. The amplicon_probe rule does an in-silico PCR with two Cutadapt passes over SILVA's training set as downloaded (silva_train_raw on SILVA 144, silva_train on 138.2):

  1. keep the reference sequences in which the forward primer matches, trimming it and everything upstream of it (-g file:<fwd> --discard-untrimmed);
  2. of those, keep the ones in which the reverse complement of the reverse primer matches, trimming it and everything downstream (-a file:<rev_rc> --discard-untrimmed --minimum-length 30).

Neither match is anchored, because SILVA holds whole 16S genes and the primers bind inside them; a match anchored to the sequence ends would find nothing. Each pass strips the flanking gene sequence the primers would never have amplified, so what survives both is the amplicon body itself. Primer mismatches are tolerated at amplicon.cutadapt.max_error_rate (default 0.2).

Chloroplast, mitochondrial and eukaryote references are then left out of the length statistics (marker pack field probe_exclude_taxa). Bacterial primers amplify organelle SSU in silico too, often with long insertions, but those are not what a 16S survey measures, and the taxon filter removes them from the results anyway. SILVA 144 holds about eight times more organelle sequences than 138.2, enough to drag the statistic along: for 799F/1175R, p95 is 397 bp with them and 386 bp without. With 138.2 it is 384 bp either way. The amplicons FASTA still contains every product.

The rule then writes the length distribution — n_amplicons, min, q1, median, q3, p95, p99, max, mean, stdev, plus excluded_taxa and n_excluded — to a JSON file in the project-level cache:

refdb/cache/probe_16S_silva_v144_toGenus_excl-chloroplast-eukaryota-mitochondria_<primer_hash>.json
refdb/cache/probe_16S_silva_v144_toGenus_excl-chloroplast-eukaryota-mitochondria_<primer_hash>.amplicons.fa.gz

The excluded lineages are part of the name, so a probe computed before v2.5.0 (or with a different list) is never reused by mistake.

<primer_hash> is the first 12 hex characters of a SHA-256 over the two primer files. Different primers give a different filename, so the probe re-runs; the same primers hit the cache, which lives inside the repository and therefore survives across runs and across output directories.

Two steps consume the probe:

  • pick_trunclen takes expected_length from the statistic named in probe_length_stat.16S (default p95) and uses it in the overlap constraint.
  • dada_length_filter builds its ASV length window as [q1 − window_margin, p95 + window_margin], with window_margin defaulting to 50 bp.

The probe only runs when expected_length: auto. A fixed integer or a [min, max] range skips it entirely.

Warning

If no reference sequence carries both primers, the probe stops with an error rather than returning an empty distribution. The usual causes are a primer written in the wrong orientation for the database, or a degenerate primer that was collapsed to a single consensus sequence before being written to the FASTA — keep the IUPAC ambiguity codes, Cutadapt matches them. A low cutadapt.max_error_rate on a mismatch-tolerant primer has the same effect.

docs.title: Truncation
docs.text:
16S uses the standard quality-based truncation picker: truncLen is cut just before the position where the aggregated per-base lower quartile first falls below trunc_len.q_threshold, subject to keeping the pair mergeable —

truncR1 + truncR2 >= expected_length + min_overlap

— with trunc_len.resolve_policy deciding what happens when quality and overlap disagree.

Three checks run in a fixed sequence. First, a coverage gate caps each sample at the length trunc_len.min_read_coverage_pct (95%) of its reads still reach, so the quality search cannot pick a position most reads never get to. Only then is the quality threshold applied, and only then the overlap constraint. See Amplicon length and truncation for the full picture, and Troubleshooting for what a run looks like when the cut still lands past the real read length.

docs.title: Region extraction with Metaxa2
docs.text:
With extraction.enabled: true (the default), the target_extract rule runs Metaxa2 over the ASV sequences to keep only the part of each ASV that is genuinely small-subunit rRNA. Anything that flanks it — primer remnants, chimeric tails, non-ribosomal carry-over — is trimmed away, so the ASV lengths that reach the length filter are directly comparable to the probe distribution measured on SILVA.

Input 05.dada2/seqs.fasta and 05.dada2/seqtab_head_names.txt, from dada_seqtab Command metaxa2 -t all --fasta T --table T --plus T --silent T Output 05.dada2/seqs_extracted.fasta, 05.dada2/seqtab_extracted_head_names.txt, 05.dada2/metaxa2_extraction.results.txt, 05.dada2/metaxa2_origin.tsv Raw tool output kept under 05.dada2/metaxa2/ for inspection Consumed by dada_length_filter; assign_taxonomy reads metaxa2_origin.tsv

-t all means all domains are scanned and every extracted sequence is kept. Metaxa2 is not used to decide what is bacterial: that decision is made later, by the taxon filter, on the classified lineage. The filter does use one of Metaxa2's calls, the organelle one: ASVs that Metaxa2 places in mitochondria or chloroplast are removed (filter.organelles, below). ASVs Metaxa2 cannot extract are dropped from both the FASTA and the count table, and the drop is reported in the rule log.

For 16S the pre- and post-extraction length distributions usually look almost the same, because a clean 16S amplicon is SSU from end to end. Both are plotted in stats/dada2/asv_length_hist.png, which makes an unexpected difference easy to spot.

docs.title: Metaxa2's two origin calls
docs.text:
The organelle filter uses the second answer only, collected per ASV in 05.dada2/metaxa2_origin.tsv. The difference matters most when you open the Metaxa2 files yourself to ask how much chloroplast and mitochondrial carry-over a run had, because the raw output under 05.dada2/metaxa2/ answers that question twice and the two answers can differ widely.

First pass — the HMM screen. Metaxa2 begins by sliding profile HMMs along each sequence to decide, cheaply, whether it is small-subunit rRNA at all and where the gene starts and stops. The job of this pass is to find the rRNA and mark its edges, not to identify it. Its verdict is the single letter in column 3 of seqs.extraction.results (B, A, E, C, M, O for bacteria, archaea, eukaryota, chloroplast, mitochondria, other) and the block of seqs.summary.txt headed "SSU rRNA sequences by preliminary origin". Metaxa2 itself labels this call preliminary.

Second pass — the BLAST refinement. The extracted regions are then aligned against Metaxa2's reference database and classified on the alignment. This is the call to use. It is what lands in seqs.taxonomy.txt, in the per-origin FASTAs (seqs.bacteria.fasta, seqs.mitochondria.fasta, and so on), and in the block of seqs.summary.txt headed "Number of SSU rRNA sequences assigned to each origin".

On the 16S test set (PRJNA305879, six samples, default settings), Metaxa2 recognised 228 ASVs as SSU rRNA:

Origin First pass, HMM screen Second pass, after BLAST Bacteria 69 195 Chloroplast 55 0 Mitochondria 104 29 Uncertain — 4

By the first pass, 46% of these ASVs are mitochondrial and 24% chloroplast; by the second, 86% are bacterial and none is chloroplast.

The second reading is the correct one, and the disagreement is expected rather than a malfunction. Chloroplasts and mitochondria descend from free-living bacteria and their SSU genes still look bacterial, so the organellar HMM profiles and the bacterial ones overlap heavily. A fast profile scan cannot separate them; an alignment against full-length references can. The screen is deliberately permissive because its purpose is to avoid missing rRNA, not to name it.

These are ASV counts, not read counts

Every number above counts distinct sequences. On the same test set the 29 mitochondrial ASVs are 13% of the 226 ASVs that reach the taxon filter, but they carry 1.5% of the reads (2,984 of 196,081): organellar ASVs are often numerous but individually rare, and in a root or leaf sample it can be the reverse. To weight by reads, use 06.taxonomy/asv_table_unfiltered.txt: it has Metaxa2's call (metaxa2_origin) next to the per-sample counts of every ASV, the removed ones included (see the table with everything). asv_table.txt will not do, because the organelle filter has already removed the ASVs Metaxa2 calls mitochondria or chloroplast.

docs.title: Taxonomy
docs.text:
amplicon.taxonomy.method picks one of two classifiers. Both read the length-filtered ASVs (05.dada2/seqs_lenfilt.fasta plus the matching seqtab_lenfilt_head_names.txt), both apply the same taxon filter, and both write the same four tables into 06.taxonomy/: the three filtered ones and asv_table_unfiltered.txt, which lists every ASV with Metaxa2's call and what the filter did to it.

rdp sintax Tool DADA2 assignTaxonomy, then addSpecies vsearch --sintax Reference silva_train + silva_species silva_sintax Confidence setting min_boot: 80 sintax_cutoff: 0.8 Reverse complement try_rc: true --strand both, always Deepest rank returned Species, as a binomial Genus Conda environment workflow/envs/taxonomy.yaml workflow/envs/vsearch.yaml Reproducibility fixed by amplicon.seed, apart from DADA2's random tie-breaking (rare, see Troubleshooting) fixed by amplicon.seed, at any thread count

The RDP path classifies the unique ASV sequences and then expands the result back so every ASV ID gets its own row — extraction can leave two ASVs with an identical trimmed sequence, and this keeps them from being classified twice.

VSEARCH SINTAX needs about 2–3 GB regardless of how many ASVs are in the table, which makes it the practical choice on large runs. With amplicon.seed fixed, its bootstrap confidence comes out the same at any thread count, because VSEARCH 2.32, the version MetaFlux uses from v2.5.0 on, gives every ASV its own random stream.

docs.title: The species step (16S only)
docs.text:
silva_train stops at genus, so the RDP path alone cannot name a species. 16S is the only marker whose pack declares a taxonomy_species_db, and for it the rdp branch of assign_taxonomy runs DADA2's addSpecies against silva_species — a separate, species-annotated SILVA file — immediately after assignTaxonomy. MetaFlux calls it with DADA2's own defaults apart from tryRC, which follows taxonomy.try_rc (the same setting assignTaxonomy uses), so a species is added only on an unambiguous exact match; ASVs with no match, or with more than one, keep an empty species slot.

addSpecies returns the bare epithet (subtilis), not the full binomial, and the Species column of taxon_seq_table.txt keeps it as it is (see reading the tables in R for building the binomial there). The 16S pack sets prefix_style: bare, which tells the taxonomy-string builder two things: add the rank prefixes itself, and render the last slot as a Genus + species binomial by gluing the genus back on. A finished 16S lineage on SILVA 144 therefore reads (on SILVA 138.2 the same, without the k__ slot):

d__Bacteria;k__Bacillati;p__Bacillota;c__Bacilli;o__Bacillales;f__Bacillaceae;g__Bacillus;s__Bacillus subtilis

Under sintax there is no species rank at all. The SINTAX database is converted from the same toGenus training set and carries only the ranks down to genus (d: to g:; seven on SILVA 144, six on 138.2), so the Species column of taxon_seq_table.txt is NA for every ASV and no s__ segment appears in the taxonomy string. Species-level 16S calls require method: rdp, and under sintax a filter token with the s__ prefix stops the run at start-up, because it could never match.

Tip

Species assignment from a single 16S region is exact-match only and often absent — that is the method, not a failure of the run. Where species resolution is the point of the experiment, the two protein-coding markers are the alternative: gyrB has higher intra-genus resolution than 16S, and rpoB assigns far more ASVs to species than 16S V3–V4 does.

The prefixes are keyed to what a rank means: the domain is written d__ and, on SILVA 144, the kingdom k__, under both methods, whatever letters the SINTAX file uses internally. A keep: [d__Bacteria] token therefore behaves identically whichever method is selected (see domain and kingdom, above).

docs.title: Keeping and discarding taxa
docs.text:
The keep and discard lists have no built-in default — they are commented out in the shipped config on purpose, so a run that forgets them applies no tokens rather than silently applying another marker's. The organelle filter (below) is on by default and needs no tokens, so it still runs. The recommended 16S starting point:

taxonomy:
  filter:
    enabled: true
    keep:    [d__Bacteria, d__Archaea]
    discard: [o__Chloroplast, f__Mitochondria]
  • keep runs first and defines what survives. [d__Bacteria, d__Archaea] keeps prokaryotes and drops both off-target eukaryotic hits and ASVs that stayed unclassified at domain level.
  • discard then prunes what is left. Chloroplast and mitochondrial 16S are amplified by most universal primers from any plant, algal or host material in the sample, and they are ribosomal enough to pass Metaxa2 — the filter is where they go.
  • Lab and kit contaminants a negative control revealed can be added to discard as further genus tokens, e.g. [o__Chloroplast, f__Mitochondria, g__Ralstonia].
  • ASVs that Metaxa2 calls mitochondria or chloroplast are removed as well (filter.organelles: metaxa2, the default; off keeps them), and every ASV is still listed, with Metaxa2's call, in 06.taxonomy/asv_table_unfiltered.txt — see the organelle filter.

Each token is matched against a whole rank segment of the taxonomy string, so g__Bacillus matches a genus named exactly that and never a substring somewhere else in the lineage (a SILVA 144 --other suffix is ignored, see above). A token that can never match a 16S string stops the run at start-up, before any step: one written for MetaFlux v2.4.0 or earlier (k__Bacteria, now d__Bacteria), a k__ token on SILVA 138.2, or a name that cannot stand in its slot (k__Fungi); see when MetaFlux refuses a token at start-up. If the filter removes every ASV after the classification, MetaFlux stops with an error instead of writing an empty table — that combination nearly always means the tokens belong to a different marker.

discard also looks one step past the reported taxonomy. The reported lineage stops at the last rank whose confidence reaches min_boot / sintax_cutoff, and mitochondrial 16S often stays below that at order and family level although the classifier's best hit is clearly Mitochondria — plant and algal mitochondria are diverse, and SILVA 144 holds many more of them than 138.2. Such an ASV is reported as p__Pseudomonadota, escapes f__Mitochondria, and turns up in the abundance table and, as a very long branch, in the tree. So an ASV is also discarded when its best hit carries a discard token at the token's own rank with at least filter.discard_min_support support (default 50, in percent; SINTAX confidences count ×100). Each such ASV is listed in the log with its support. discard_min_support: null switches the check off.

On the 16S test set, with the recommended filter above and otherwise default settings, this check removed 6 ASVs: all were reported only to phylum (p__Pseudomonadota), all had Mitochondria as best hit, and Metaxa2 called all of them mitochondrial. Full behaviour on Keeping and discarding taxa.

Plant mitochondria that no token catches

On the 16S test set (PRJNA305879, plant-associated), some mitochondrial ASVs got past every token: 13 ASVs (1,421 reads) with rdp on SILVA 144, 10 (1,292 reads) with either method on SILVA 138.2, and 3 (7 reads) with sintax on SILVA 144, the default. rdp reported most of them as Enterobacterales, some down to genus. Their best hit is another taxon, or Mitochondria with support below discard_min_support, so neither the tokens nor the best-hit check can catch them. Metaxa2 still calls them mitochondrial, and the organelle filter removes them on that call, so at the default settings they are gone whichever classifier and release you use. With filter.organelles: off they stay in the table.

docs.title: What a 16S run produces
docs.text:
The final tables are in 06.taxonomy/:

File Rows Contents asv_table.txt ASV_# IDs per-sample counts plus a taxonomy column asv_table_seqs.txt ASV sequences the same table, keyed by sequence taxon_seq_table.txt ASV_# IDs one column per rank plus the sequence: Domain, Kingdom, Phylum … Species on SILVA 144; Domain, Phylum … Species on SILVA 138.2 asv_table_unfiltered.txt ASV_# IDs, every ASV that reached the filter the same counts and taxonomy, plus Metaxa2's call (metaxa2_origin) and filter_status: kept, or the filter step that removed the ASV

Alongside them, stats/taxonomy_reference_check.json records what the reference check saw in the SILVA file, stats/trunclen.json records the truncation decision, stats/dada2/asv_length_stats.json and asv_length_hist.png record the ASV length distributions before extraction, after extraction and after the length filter, and stats/read_tracking.txt shows how many reads each sample kept at every stage. The full layout is in Output files.

16S is also the only marker with an optional phylogeny stage: switch it on and the run adds a maximum-likelihood tree of the retained ASVs, exported unrooted, for Faith's PD and UniFrac in R. It is off by default and adds nothing to the run when it stays off. See Phylogeny (16S).

docs.title: 18S rRNA (eukaryotes)
docs.text:
The 18S small-subunit rRNA gene is the eukaryotic counterpart of 16S: one conserved gene, present in every eukaryote, with variable regions (V4, V9) that carry enough signal to separate protists, microalgae, fungi and small metazoans. In MetaFlux it is the marker of choice for surveying eukaryotic diversity in soil, water, gut and plant material.

Read proportions are not cell proportions, and 18S is worse than 16S here

Every rRNA-gene survey is distorted by gene copy number, but the scale of the problem differs by orders of magnitude between the two markers. Bacterial genomes carry roughly 1–20 copies of the 16S gene, about a tenfold spread. Eukaryotic rDNA is arranged in tandem arrays whose copy number ranges from a handful to tens of thousands per genome, with ciliates and some dinoflagellates at the extreme end.

A ciliate carrying thousands of copies and a small flagellate carrying a few can be equally abundant as cells and differ by three orders of magnitude in reads. Treat an 18S table as a comparison of the same taxon between samples, not as a census of relative cell abundance within one sample. Copy-number correction for protists is not generally available, so compare composition between samples processed in the same way.

From raw FASTQ to ASVs the path is the same as for every other amplicon marker — primer removal, truncation, DADA2 denoising, merging, chimera removal. Two things are specific to 18S, and both are handled by the marker pack workflow/markers/18S.yaml:

  • the length probe and the taxonomy come from different databases;
  • the taxonomy reference ships two files that disagree on how many ranks they carry.

Neither needs manual intervention beyond setting the marker type and the taxon filter.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
Set type: 18S and supply the 18S primers. A minimal amplicon block:

amplicon:
  type: 18S
  primers:
    fwd: /path/to/fwd_primer.fasta
    rev: /path/to/rev_primer.fasta
    orientation: fixed

  expected_length: auto
  probe_length_stat:
    18S: p95

  extraction:
    enabled: false          # 18S has no region extractor

  taxonomy:
    method: sintax          # rdp | sintax — both are available for 18S
    filter:
      enabled: true
      keep:    [d__Eukaryota]
      discard: []
Setting Why it is here type: 18S Selects the marker pack, and with it both reference databases, the rank models, and the "no extractor" fact. expected_length: auto Lets the in-silico PCR probe size the amplicon window from the primers actually supplied. Fine for every V4 pair on a long enough read budget; not for V9 — see the primer table below. auto resolves to the statistic named in probe_length_stat (p95 by default), not to the typical amplicon length. For TAReuk V4 on SILVA-Euk that is ~494 bp against a 381 bp median, so the merge-overlap constraint asks for truncLen_R1 + truncLen_R2 ≥ 506 bp. A 2×300 run clears that comfortably; a 2×250 run has only ~462 bp left after primer trimming and stops at pick_trunclen. On a tight read budget, either set probe_length_stat.18S: median (or q3), or give expected_length a number of its own. probe_length_stat.18S Which statistic of the probed length distribution becomes the resolved expected_length — the single amplicon size used for the truncLen/overlap constraint. p95 is the shipped default: 18S V4 has a ragged upper tail, and p95 keeps it permissive without chasing the outliers that p99 would include. The ASV length-filter window is a separate calculation — in auto mode it uses the probe's q1 and p95 when a probe has run, and falls back to expected_length ±15% when none has, see below. The key is required for 18S whether or not expected_length is auto — if it is missing the workflow stops at start-up with a message naming it. extraction.enabled: false There is no 18S region extractor. Left true it is forced off with a warning, so this is a tidiness setting rather than a functional one. taxonomy.filter.keep The keep/discard lists have no built-in default. A 16S list here would discard every eukaryotic ASV, so the marker's own tokens have to be set explicitly.

Both classifiers work for 18S: rdp (DADA2 assignTaxonomy against the PR2 DADA2 file) and sintax (VSEARCH against the PR2 UTAX file, with its domain moved to the SINTAX letter d: so that VSEARCH classifies the domain first; see below). See Keeping and discarding taxa for how the two paths are made to behave identically.

docs.title: Two databases, two jobs
docs.text:
18S is the one marker where the database that measures amplicon length is not the database that assigns names.

Database Role in an 18S run Why SILVA-Eukaryotic 18S v132 In-silico PCR probe substrate only — never used for taxonomy It recovers 96–97% of its references for every V4 primer pair tested, against 66–75% for PR2. A probe that finds nearly every reference sizes the length window from the real amplicon distribution rather than from whichever subset happened to match. PR2 v5.1.1 Taxonomy reference (both rdp and sintax) The better-curated eukaryote/protist reference. It is not eukaryote-only — see below.

PR2 also carries prokaryotic and organellar references, which is useful

Counted directly in the file the workflow downloads (240,201 references):

Domain field References Eukaryota 223,210 Bacteria 8,028 Eukaryota:plas (plastid) 6,765 Eukaryota:mito (mitochondrial) 1,890 Eukaryota:nucl (nucleomorph) 148 Archaea 131 Eukaryota:apic (apicoplast) 22 Eukaryota:chro (chromatophore) 7

Eukaryotic primers are not eukaryote-specific: they also amplify bacterial SSU and organellar (plastid, mitochondrial) rRNA, which is exactly why PR2 carries dedicated Bacteria, plastid and mitochondrial entries in the table above rather than omitting them. Because PR2 can name those products, they are assigned to those references and not to the nearest eukaryote, and keep: [d__Eukaryota] then removes them. It removes the nucleomorph, apicoplast and chromatophore entries too, since their domain field is not plain Eukaryota either; add them to keep if they belong to your study, for example keep: [d__Eukaryota, d__Eukaryota:nucl].

PR2 files its prokaryotes into the same eukaryote-style ranks, with older phylum names: a bacterial ASV reads, for example, d__Bacteria;sg__Terrabacteria;dv__Firmicutes-Firmicutes_X;… under sintax. Do not expect these names to match those of a 16S table.

Three files are fetched on first use and cached under refdb/, and a fourth is built from one of them. The three downloads are plain files, so their fetch rules are generated from the pack — there is no 18S-specific download code in the workflow. The fourth, pr2_sintax, is PR2's UTAX file with its domain moved to the SINTAX letter d: (see below); rule convert_pr2_sintax builds it when a sintax run needs it and it is missing, and again whenever pr2_utax or the conversion script is newer than it.

Pack symbol Cached at Source silva_euk refdb/silva_euk/silva_132.18s.dada2.fa.gz Zenodo record 1447330 pr2_dada2 refdb/pr2/pr2_SSU_dada2.fasta.gz PR2 GitHub release v5.1.1 pr2_utax refdb/pr2/pr2_SSU_UTAX.fasta.gz PR2 GitHub release v5.1.1 pr2_sintax refdb/pr2/pr2_SSU_UTAX_domain-first.fasta.gz built from pr2_utax by rule convert_pr2_sintax (method: sintax only)

Nothing about these needs declaring in a run config. An entry under references: is only needed to relocate one — for example to point at a shared copy on a cluster filesystem instead of the project-local refdb/.

PR2 carries species names inside the trainset itself, so the DADA2 addSpecies step that 16S uses does not run here (taxonomy_species_db is null in the pack). Species assignments come straight out of the main classification.

The probe result is cached per primer pair, keyed by a hash of the two primer FASTA files, at refdb/cache/probe_18S_silva_euk_18s_v132_<hash>.json. Changing the primers changes the hash and re-probes automatically; reusing the same primers across runs reuses the cached measurement. Details in Amplicon length and truncation.

docs.title: No region extractor
docs.text:
16S runs can pass their ASVs through Metaxa2 and ITS runs through ITSx, trimming each ASV back to the marker region before the length filter sees it. MetaFlux has no equivalent step for 18S — Metaxa2 can handle SSU, but it is deliberately not wired in here — so extractor is none in the pack.

Because no rule produces an extracted FASTA, leaving extraction.enabled: true would make the workflow ask for a file nothing creates. Instead it is forced off at start-up, with a warning on stderr:

[MetaFlux] warning: marker 18S has no target-region extractor; ignoring
amplicon.extraction.enabled: true (no extraction step will run)

The consequences are small:

  • The ASV length filter still runs, on the post-DADA2 sequences rather than on extracted ones. In auto mode its window is [probe_q1 − window_margin, probe_p95 + window_margin].
  • Taxonomy is assigned from 05.dada2/seqs_lenfilt.fasta, the length-filtered ASVs, as it is for every marker.
  • Flanking conserved sequence that an extractor would have trimmed stays on the ASV. Since the probe measures the same primer-defined fragment, probe distribution and ASV distribution remain comparable, which is what the length filter needs.

docs.title: PR2 ships two rank depths
docs.text:
The two PR2 release files do not describe taxonomy at the same depth. Verified against v5.1.1:

PR2 file Used by Ranks Rank names pr2_SSU_dada2.fasta.gz method: rdp 9 Domain; Supergroup; Division; Subdivision; Class; Order; Family; Genus; Species pr2_SSU_UTAX.fasta.gz method: sintax, through a copy with the domain first (see below) 8 Domain; Supergroup; Division+Subdivision merged into one field; Class; Order; Family; Genus; Species

Most markers use one rank model for both classifiers. 18S declares two — tax_levels for the rdp path and sintax_tax_levels for the sintax path — so each classifier is told the true depth of the file it is reading. If the depth were left at DADA2's default of seven ranks (Kingdom to Species), assignTaxonomy would still return all nine PR2 columns — it sizes its output from the reference, not from the rank names it was handed — but it names those columns from taxLevels, so only the first seven would get names, and they would be the wrong ones. PR2's Supergroup would be labelled Phylum, its Family labelled Species, and Genus and Species would never reach the taxonomy string at all. DADA2 would report no error.

Rank prefixes are keyed to what a rank means, not to the letters the underlying file happens to use. PR2's UTAX file labels its ranks k:, d:, p:, c: …, with the Domain under k: and the Supergroup under d::

>AB353770.1.1740_U;tax=k:Eukaryota,d:TSAR,p:Alveolata-Dinoflagellata,c:Dinophyceae,…

VSEARCH does not read SINTAX letters as names. It reads them as a fixed top-down order, d, k, p, c, o, f, g, s, and counts the confidence of a rank only over the bootstrap rounds that agreed on every rank above it. On the file as published, the Supergroup would be VSEARCH's top rank and the Domain would sit below it, so an ASV whose Supergroup stayed under sintax_cutoff would lose its Domain too, even when nearly every round agreed on it. MetaFlux therefore classifies against a copy of the file with the two letters swapped, the Domain under d: and the Supergroup under k:. Rule convert_pr2_sintax builds the copy, headers only, with the sequences untouched; it stops on a file that does not have PR2 5.1.1's letter order, so a future PR2 release with a different layout is noticed rather than misread.

For ASV_71 of the 18S test set (PRJDB12231), whose best hit in PR2 v5.1.1 is Angulamoeba microcystivorans (Amoebozoa), VSEARCH's confidences read:

letters as published : d:Amoebozoa(0.66),k:Eukaryota(0.66),p:Evosea-Evosea_X(0.66),…
domain first         : d:Eukaryota(1.00),k:Amoebozoa(0.66),p:Evosea-Evosea_X(0.66),…

With sintax_cutoff: 0.8 the first gives the ASV no taxonomy at all; the second gives it d__Eukaryota. Nothing below the domain changes.

The tables render the Domain as d__ and the Supergroup as sg__, to match the rdp output. Only the raw VSEARCH output, 06.taxonomy/_sintax_raw.tsv, shows the swapped letters, as in the second line above: there d: holds the domain and k: the supergroup. The taxonomy string of a dinoflagellate ASV reads, under the two methods:

rdp    : d__Eukaryota;sg__TSAR;dv__Alveolata;sbd__Dinoflagellata;c__Dinophyceae;…
sintax : d__Eukaryota;sg__TSAR;dv__Alveolata-Dinoflagellata;c__Dinophyceae;…

Only the merged Division/Subdivision field differs. Everything above and below it is identical, which is why a d__, sg__, c__ … s__ token behaves the same under either method. A Division token does not: under rdp, dv__ holds the Division alone (dv__Opisthokonta), while under sintax it holds Division and Subdivision joined by "-" (dv__Opisthokonta-Fungi), so dv__Opisthokonta matches nothing on a sintax run, and dv__Opisthokonta-Fungi nothing on an rdp run. The start-up check of the filter tokens cannot see this, because the joined form is a property of PR2's names, not of the rank, so check a dv__ token against the taxonomy column of a run made with the same method. sbd__ exists only under rdp: under sintax an sbd__ token stops the run at start-up.

Full prefix set, in order:

Rank Prefix Present under rdp Present under sintax Domain d__ yes yes Supergroup sg__ yes yes Division dv__ yes merged into dv__ Subdivision sbd__ yes merged into dv__ Class c__ yes yes Order o__ yes yes Family f__ yes yes Genus g__ yes yes Species s__ yes yes

Rank columns in the output tables

06.taxonomy/taxon_seq_table.txt has one column per rank, so an rdp run of 18S produces nine rank columns and a sintax run eight. The taxonomy string column in asv_table.txt is built from the prefixes above and is directly comparable between the two. Scripts that assume a fixed set of seven ranks will need adjusting for this marker; pick the rank columns by name — see reading the tables in R.

PR2 already stores species as complete Genus_species binomials. On the rdp path the string builder recognises this and emits them as they are, instead of gluing the genus on a second time the way it does for a bare lowercase SILVA epithet.

docs.title: Setting the taxon filter
docs.text:
The keep/discard lists are rank-aware token lists with no hidden default: whatever is listed is exactly what is applied. For 18S the sensible starting point is

taxonomy:
  filter:
    enabled: true
    keep:    [d__Eukaryota]
    discard: []

Each token is matched against a whole ;-delimited segment of the taxonomy string, so d__Eukaryota matches the Domain field and nothing else. keep runs first and defines what survives; discard then prunes what is left.

A 16S filter on an 18S run

A 16S keep list written for MetaFlux v2.4.0 or earlier, [k__Bacteria, k__Archaea], stops the run at start-up, before any step: 18S tables have no k__ slot. The current 16S list, keep: [d__Bacteria, d__Archaea], does pass that check, because PR2 holds bacteria and archaea too, and then keeps only the few prokaryotic ASVs, removing every eukaryotic one. Should a list remove every ASV, the workflow stops with an error naming the marker and the number of ASVs removed, rather than write a header-only table. Either message almost always means the filter lists were copied from another marker.

keep also removes the unclassified

An ASV that SINTAX or RDP left unassigned at Domain has no d__ segment, so a keep: [d__Eukaryota] list drops it along with any genuine off-target sequence. Such ASVs are few (1 of 1,268 on the 18S test set, PRJDB12231, with sintax): both classifiers judge the domain on its own (for sintax this is what the swapped letters above are for), so an ASV that cannot be placed in a supergroup usually still reads d__Eukaryota. keep: [] keeps every ASV. Which is right depends on whether unassigned ASVs are noise or the interesting part of the dataset.

To drop lab or kit contaminants that a negative control revealed, add them to discard using the exact rank-prefixed name as it appears in the taxonomy column of asv_table.txt. More on both directions in Keeping and discarding taxa.

docs.title: Amplicon length by primer pair
docs.text:
Expected amplicon length is a property of the primers, not of the marker. The figures below were measured in silico against SILVA-Euk across the common eukaryotic pairs:

Region Primer pair Core length Read budget needed to merge expected_length V4 TAReuk454FWD1 / TAReukREV3 ~380 bp 2×300 auto V4 Parfrey 515F / 1119r ~565 bp beyond 2×300 auto V4 Hadziavdic 566F / 1200R ~595 bp beyond 2×300 auto V4 515Y / 926R (V4–V5 in 16S nomenclature) ~551 bp beyond 2×300 auto V9 Euk1391F / EukBr ~130 bp any manual, e.g. [115, 150]

"Core length" is the amplicon between the primers, after primer trimming. The spread across pairs is wide — 380 to 595 bp for V4 alone — which is exactly why the probe measures the actual pair rather than assuming a marker-wide number.

Three of these pairs cannot be merged on a standard paired-end run

The overlap constraint is truncLen_R1 + truncLen_R2 ≥ expected_length + min_overlap. A 2×300 run leaves roughly 560 bp once the primers are trimmed off both reads, so only the shortest V4 pair clears it:

Primer pair Constraint at p95 2×250 (~460 bp) 2×300 (~560 bp) TAReuk454FWD1 / TAReukREV3 ~506 bp fails clears 515Y / 926R ~679 bp fails fails Parfrey 515F / 1119r ~692 bp fails fails Hadziavdic 566F / 1200R ~729 bp fails fails

The run does not produce a silently truncated result: pick_trunclen stops with the deficit in bp, so the problem surfaces before DADA2 is invoked. The options are a longer read length, a shorter primer pair, or accepting that the pairs will not merge. probe_length_stat.18S: median relaxes the constraint by sizing it from the typical amplicon rather than the p95 tail. With it, 515Y / 926R needs ~564 bp, which is marginal on 2×300.

V9 must be set manually

Only 41% of SILVA-Euk references (24% of PR2's) are recovered in silico for Euk1391F / EukBr. EukBr sits at the 3′ terminus of the gene and most references are truncated before it, so the reverse primer simply has nothing to match on. auto would then size the window from that biased minority rather than from the real amplicon distribution. Set an explicit range instead:

expected_length: [115, 150]

V9 is also the case to watch for truncation. The insert is only ~130 bp, so on 2×250 or 2×300 reads cutadapt's 3′ pass trims away the read-through and most reads come back at about that length — while on a clean run pick_trunclen has no quality drop to cut on and takes the ceiling instead, potentially a hundred bases past the end of the amplicon. filterAndTrim discards every read shorter than truncLen, which would be all of them.

trunc_len.min_read_coverage_pct should prevent that overshoot: it caps the ceiling at the length 95% of reads reach, and after the 3′ trim that length is the amplicon length itself. V9 is not covered by the 18S test set (Test datasets), so verify rather than assume: check the ceilings reported in logs/pick_trunclen.log against the post-trimming read lengths. Setting trunc_len.mode: manual with manual_r1 / manual_r2 just below the post-trimming length remains the safe choice for a marker this short. The failure mode and its diagnosis are under Troubleshooting.

Write the TAReuk primers with the IUPAC ambiguity codes published by Stoeck et al. (2010). With the codes replaced by single bases, reads that carry the other base at those positions are trimmed only because cutadapt tolerates mismatches (amplicon.cutadapt.max_error_rate, 0.2 by default).

docs.title: What the run produces
docs.text:
Same layout as any other amplicon run. The 18S-specific parts:

File Contents refdb/cache/probe_18S_silva_euk_18s_v132_<hash>.json Probed amplicon-length distribution for this primer pair, against SILVA-Euk 05.dada2/seqs_lenfilt.fasta Length-filtered ASVs, straight from DADA2 since no extraction runs 06.taxonomy/asv_table.txt Counts per sample plus one PR2 taxonomy string per ASV 06.taxonomy/taxon_seq_table.txt One column per rank — nine under rdp, eight under sintax 06.taxonomy/_sintax_raw.tsv sintax only: the raw VSEARCH output, with the domain under d: and the supergroup under k: (written sg__ in the tables)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Reproduced from the MetaFlux reference list:

  • Quast, C., et al. (2013). The SILVA ribosomal RNA gene database project. Nucleic Acids Research.
  • Guillou, L., et al. (2013). The Protist Ribosomal Reference database (PR2): a catalog of unicellular eukaryote small sub-unit rRNA sequences with curated taxonomy. Nucleic Acids Research. (database v5.1.1 — https://github.com/pr2database/pr2database)
  • Stoeck, T., et al. (2010). Multiple marker parallel tag environmental DNA sequencing reveals a highly complex eukaryotic community in marine anoxic water. Molecular Ecology. (18S V4 primers TAReuk454FWD1 / TAReukREV3)
  • Parada, A. E., Needham, D. M. & Fuhrman, J. A. (2016). Every base matters: assessing small subunit rRNA primers for marine microbiomes with mock communities, time series and global field samples. Environmental Microbiology. (18S V4 primers 515Y / 926R — the pair known as V4–V5 in 16S nomenclature)
  • Parfrey, L. W., et al. (2014). Communities of microbial eukaryotes in the mammalian gut within the context of environmental eukaryotic diversity. Frontiers in Microbiology. (18S V4 primers 515F / 1119r)
  • Hadziavdic, K., et al. (2014). Characterization of the 18S rRNA gene for designing universal eukaryote specific primers. PLoS ONE. (18S V4 primers 566F / 1200R)
  • Amaral-Zettler, L. A., et al. (2009). A method for studying protistan diversity using massively parallel sequencing of V9 hypervariable regions of small-subunit ribosomal RNA genes. PLoS ONE. (18S V9 primers Euk1391F / EukBr)

The full list, including the tools used at every step, is on Citation and references.

docs.title: gyrB (bacterial DNA gyrase subunit B)
docs.text:
gyrB encodes the B subunit of DNA gyrase, a protein-coding single-copy gene in bacteria. Because it is protein-coding, it accumulates substitutions faster than the 16S rRNA gene, so it separates organisms inside a genus that a 16S V3–V4 amplicon leaves merged. The cost is a reference database much smaller than SILVA, and a marker that is bacterial rather than universal.

MetaFlux runs gyrB through the same amplicon path as every other marker — PhiX removal, primer trimming, DADA2 denoising, length filtering, taxonomy. Three things set it apart from the rRNA markers, all of them consequences of its reference database (workflow/markers/gyrB.yaml declares them): the reference is already amplicon-length, only the RDP classifier is available, and the reference carries a built-in paralog tag. The first needs no attention at all; the other two need one config line each.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: amplicon.type gyrB (also accepted as gyrb or GYRB — matched case-insensitively) Reference database DD7RZ8 v6, the INRAE gyrB DADA2 trainset built on GTDB r226 Role of that database both the taxonomy reference and the amplicon-length probe substrate Probe mode direct — lengths read straight off the reference Classifier RDP only (amplicon.taxonomy.method: rdp) Separate species step none — the trainset itself carries species Region extractor none (no gyrB equivalent of Metaxa2 or ITSx) Rank model Gene;Phylum;Class;Order;Family;Genus;Species Primers none are shipped; Barret 2015 F64 / R353 is the pair the reference was built with

docs.title: Setting up a run
docs.text:
Set the marker type, point at the primer FASTAs, and choose the RDP classifier. A minimal gyrB block looks like this:

mode: amplicon

amplicon:
  type: gyrB
  primers:
    fwd: /path/to/gyrB_F64.fasta
    rev: /path/to/gyrB_R353.fasta
    orientation: fixed          # fixed | mixed
  expected_length: auto
  probe_length_stat:
    16S: p95                    # gyrB reads this key — see "Amplicon length" below
  extraction:
    enabled: false              # no gyrB region extractor
  taxonomy:
    method: rdp                 # gyrB has no SINTAX build
    min_boot: 80
    try_rc: true
    filter:
      enabled: true
      keep:    []
      discard: []               # [other] drops paralogs — see "The paralog tag"

Primers are never supplied by MetaFlux: amplicon.primers.fwd and amplicon.primers.rev must both point at existing FASTA files, and the run stops at start-up if either is missing. The Barret 2015 F64 / R353 pair is the natural choice, because DD7RZ8's reference amplicons were cut with those same primers, but any gyrB pair works — the length window is measured from the reference rather than assumed.

The shipped config template defaults to method: sintax

config/config.yaml ships with amplicon.taxonomy.method: sintax, which is fine for 16S/ITS/18S but not available for gyrB. A run config copied from the template without changing that line stops at start-up, before any compute is spent:

[MetaFlux] marker gyrB has no SINTAX reference database, so
amplicon.taxonomy.method: sintax is not available for it. Use method: rdp.

docs.title: The reference database
docs.text:
DD7RZ8 v6 is a gyrB trainset in DADA2 format, built at INRAE on GTDB release r226. It is downloaded on first use and cached, so later runs reuse it.

Cached at refdb/gyrb/train_set_gyrB_v6.fa.gz Source Recherche Data Gouv (INRAE Dataverse) file-access endpoint, https://entrepot.recherche.data.gouv.fr/api/access/datafile/760120 Fetch rule fetch_gyrb_dada2, generated from the URL in the marker pack Log <out_dir>/logs/refdb/fetch_gyrb_dada2.log

The download is a single plain .fa.gz file, so no rule was written by hand for it: MetaFlux generates one fetch rule per plain-download reference declared by the active marker pack. The URL is a Dataverse API endpoint that redirects to the object store, which wget follows.

The cache root is references.refdb_root (default refdb). An entry under references is only needed to relocate a database that already exists elsewhere on disk — for gyrB that entry is:

references:
  gyrb:
    dada2: /shared/dbs/train_set_gyrB_v6.fa.gz

Every reference sequence is one primer-trimmed in-silico amplicon, not a full-length gene, and the header is a GTDB lineage whose ranks already carry their prefixes, preceded by a bare gene tag:

>{gene};p__Phylum;c__Class;o__Order;f__Family;g__Genus;s__Genus_species

Because the prefixes are already in the reference, the marker pack sets prefix_style: embedded and MetaFlux emits each rank value verbatim instead of prepending its own p__/c__/… — the species slot stays a GTDB binomial such as s__Actinotalea_bogoriensis.

docs.title: Amplicon length: measured directly, not by in-silico PCR
docs.text:
For 16S, 18S and rpoB the amplicon-length probe runs an in-silico PCR: two passes of cutadapt against a full-length reference, keeping the sequences that carry the forward primer at the 5′ end and the reverse complement of the reverse primer at the 3′ end. That is impossible against DD7RZ8, whose sequences have already had those primer sites cut off upstream — the PCR would find nothing to match and return almost no amplicons.

So the gyrB pack sets probe_mode: direct: cutadapt is not run at all, and the length distribution is read straight from the reference sequences. Measured across the shipped DD7RZ8 v6 file, that distribution is tight — median 247 bp, minimum 234 bp, maximum 270 bp — which is exactly what a pre-trimmed amplicon reference should look like.

The probe only runs when amplicon.expected_length: auto. It writes its statistics to a JSON file whose name encodes the marker, the reference tag and a 12-character hash of both primer FASTAs:

refdb/cache/probe_gyrB_gyrb_dd7rz8_v6_<primer_hash>.json

Changing primers changes the hash, so the probe reruns; keeping the same primers across runs reuses the cached result. That JSON then feeds two downstream steps: pick_trunclen, which uses the resolved expected length to enforce the forward/reverse overlap constraint on truncLen, and the ASV length filter, which builds its auto window from the probe's q1 and p95 plus length_filter.window_margin. See Amplicon length and truncation for both.

gyrB reads probe_length_stat.16S, not a key of its own

Which statistic of the probe distribution becomes expected_length is chosen by amplicon.probe_length_stat.<key>, and the gyrB pack deliberately reuses the 16S key rather than defining a separate one. If the 16S entry is missing, the run stops at start-up with:

[MetaFlux] amplicon.probe_length_stat is missing the '16S' key that marker gyrB
needs. Add it, e.g.
    probe_length_stat:
      16S: p95

The key is checked at start-up for every non-ITS marker, whether or not expected_length is auto. A manual expected_length (a single integer, or a [min, max] pair) skips the probe itself, but the 16S entry must still be present.

docs.title: Taxonomy: RDP only
docs.text:
The DD7RZ8 release ships a DADA2 trainset and nothing else — there is no SINTAX-formatted build of it — so the marker pack leaves taxonomy_sintax_db empty and MetaFlux refuses method: sintax at start-up rather than failing later inside the classifier.

Classification is DADA2's assignTaxonomy (the RDP naive Bayesian classifier) against the trainset, with taxonomy.min_boot as the bootstrap confidence minimum and taxonomy.try_rc deciding whether reverse-complemented sequences are also tried. There is no separate addSpecies step: unlike 16S, where species come from a second SILVA file, the gyrB trainset is itself labelled to species, so the classifier reaches the species rank directly. amplicon.seed fixes the bootstrap RNG, so RDP results are reproducible run to run, apart from DADA2's random tie-breaking between equally good reference lineages, which can move a bootstrap value between identical runs (see Troubleshooting).

The classifier writes seven rank columns, taken from the marker pack:

Slot Rank column Prefix in the taxonomy string 1 Gene none — a bare gyrB or other tag 2 Phylum p__ 3 Class c__ 4 Order o__ 5 Family f__ 6 Genus g__ 7 Species s__

docs.title: The paralog tag
docs.text:
DNA gyrase subunit B has a close relative, topoisomerase IV subunit B (parE), similar enough that gyrB primers co-amplify it. DD7RZ8 handles this by labelling every reference sequence in its first rank slot: gyrB for the true gene, other for a co-amplified paralog such as parE.

MetaFlux keeps that tag as an ordinary taxonomy rank, which means paralogs can be removed with the same keep/discard filter used to drop chloroplast and mitochondrial ASVs from a 16S run:

amplicon:
  taxonomy:
    filter:
      enabled: true
      discard: [other]     # not the same as keep: [gyrB] — see below

Filter tokens are matched against whole segments of the taxonomy string, so other matches the gene tag and only the gene tag — never a substring somewhere inside a species name. Because the tag carries no rank prefix, the token is written bare, unlike the prefixed tokens (d__Bacteria, o__Chloroplast) used for the rRNA markers. A gyrB lineage has no domain or kingdom slot: its first slot is the gene tag, then come p__ to s__. So a d__ or k__ token stops the run at start-up, and so does a bare token other than the two tags (Other or Bacteria, say). See Keeping and discarding taxa.

discard: [other] drops the paralogs, and keep: [gyrB] is not an equivalent way of writing it. An ASV the classifier could not tag at all has an empty taxonomy string, so it carries no segment for either list to match: discard leaves it in, keep throws it out, silently.

Leave the filter empty on the first run

How much other to expect depends on the primers and the samples, so there is no universal right answer and MetaFlux applies no default. Running once with empty keep/discard lists makes the paralog fraction visible in the output — count the ASVs whose taxonomy string starts with other, or read the Gene column of 06.taxonomy/taxon_seq_table.txt — and then decide whether to discard them.

Co-amplification of parE depends on the taxon, so the other ASVs concentrate in particular clades. On the gyrB test set (PRJNA459479, five mock communities), 74 of 237 ASVs carry the other tag, 62 of them in Bacilli, and they hold 26% of the reads. A run dominated by such groups shows a larger other fraction, so check the composition before suspecting the primers.

If a keep/discard combination removes every ASV, assign_taxonomy stops with an error instead of writing a header-only table, since that is nearly always a marker/config mismatch.

GTDB splits genera, and the filter matches whole segments exactly

DD7RZ8 v6 carries GTDB r226 taxonomy, and GTDB routinely divides a genus that is polyphyletic under NCBI into several suffixed genera — g__Pseudomonas_A, g__Pseudomonas_B, and so on. In the shipped reference, 734 of 5,207 genera carry such a suffix, and Pseudomonas alone appears as seven separate names:

g__Pseudomonas   g__Pseudomonas_B   g__Pseudomonas_E   g__Pseudomonas_M
g__Pseudomonas_O   g__Pseudomonas_P   g__Pseudomonas_T

The keep/discard filter matches whole ;-delimited segments exactly — deliberately, so that g__Bacillus can never match a substring elsewhere in a lineage. The consequence here is that discard: [g__Pseudomonas] removes only the unsuffixed genus and leaves the other six untouched, and keep: [g__Pseudomonas] keeps only that one.

Check the names actually present before writing a filter — the Genus column of 06.taxonomy/taxon_seq_table.txt shows them, without the g__ that a token needs — and list every variant that applies. This affects gyrB only: rpoB's FROGS reference carries NCBI taxonomy, where the genus is not split.

docs.title: No region extractor
docs.text:
MetaFlux has no gyrB equivalent of Metaxa2 (16S) or ITSx (ITS), so there is nothing to trim ASVs down to a target region. amplicon.extraction.enabled: true is therefore forced off for gyrB with a warning on stderr:

[MetaFlux] warning: marker gyrB has no target-region extractor; ignoring
amplicon.extraction.enabled: true (no extraction step will run)

Setting enabled: false explicitly keeps the run log clean. The ASV length filter still runs either way, so off-target amplicons of the wrong size are still removed.

docs.title: What the output looks like
docs.text:
The final tables are the same four files as for every other marker, under 06.taxonomy/ in the output directory:

File Rows Notes asv_table.txt ASV IDs per-sample counts plus one taxonomy column asv_table_seqs.txt ASV sequences the same table keyed by sequence instead of ID taxon_seq_table.txt ASV IDs one column per rank (Gene … Species) plus the sequence; the cells hold the bare names (Bacillota, Latilactobacillus_sakei), while the taxonomy strings keep the prefixes asv_table_unfiltered.txt ASV IDs, every ASV that reached the filter the counts and taxonomy before the taxon filter, plus metaxa2_origin (NA for gyrB) and filter_status; the paralogs that discard: [other] removes can still be counted here

A gyrB taxonomy string keeps the gene tag in front of the GTDB lineage:

gyrB;p__Pseudomonadota;c__Gammaproteobacteria;o__Pseudomonadales;f__Pseudomonadaceae;g__Pseudomonas;s__Pseudomonas_aeruginosa

Ranks the classifier could not assign above min_boot are simply absent from the string, so a shorter string means a less confident assignment rather than a missing rank.
