├── 04.extracted_reads/  # per-taxon reads (only when extract_taxa is set)
├── stats/               # read_tracking.txt; sylph/ summary (profiler sylph | both)
├── multiqc/             # multiqc_report.html + multiqc_data/
├── samples.tsv          # sample → source → FASTQ manifest
└── logs/                # per-rule logs

The result of a shotgun run is 03.abundance/otu_table.tsv (taxon × sample abundances) with its BIOM twin otu_table.biom, the per-sample Bracken reports next to them, and stats/read_tracking.txt. With shotgun.profiler: sylph the Kraken2 and Bracken files are not made and the result is 03.abundance/sylph_table.tsv instead; with both there are both (see below).

docs.title: 01.preprocessing/
docs.text:
The cleaned FASTQs here are temporary — Snakemake removes a file marked that way as soon as every rule that needed it has finished: _dephix goes once host removal (or fastp) has read it, _dehost once fastp has, and _trim once Kraken2 has, or sylph_sketch, or both, depending on shotgun.profiler. What persists is the QC and the counts:

File Written by Contents {sample}_fastp.html / _fastp.json trim_adapters fastp's adapter and quality trimming report. The JSON is also read by MultiQC, by the read-tracking step, and by Bracken (to pick the k-mer distribution matching the post-trim read length). {sample}_dephix_stats.txt decontam_phix BBDuk PhiX-removal counts. Only when shotgun.decontamination.remove_phix: true. {sample}_dehost_stats.txt decontam_host Surviving non-host pairs after BBMap. Only when shotgun.decontamination.host_genomes is non-empty. refs/bbmap_index/ build_host_index The BBMap index of the host reference, built once and reused for every sample. Host removal only.

The temporary FASTQs are named for the stage they came off: {sample}_dephix_R{1,2}.fastq.gz (BBDuk, PhiX) → {sample}_dehost_R{1,2}.fastq.gz (BBMap, host) → {sample}_trim_R{1,2}.fastq.gz (fastp). Each stage is optional; the chain simply skips what is switched off. The concatenated host reference refs/host_combined.fna.gz is temporary too — it is deleted once the BBMap index has been built from it. See decontamination.

docs.title: 02.classification/
docs.text:
One subfolder per profiler: kraken2/ when Kraken2 runs (shotgun.profiler: kraken2 or both) and sylph/ when sylph runs (sylph or both; see below). kraken2/ holds:

File Contents {sample}_report.txt Kraken2's tree report. {sample}_output.txt Kraken2's per-read assignment — one line per read pair. Large, and only useful for read extraction and troubleshooting. {sample}_R1.fastq.gz, _R2 The reads Kraken2 managed to classify. Kept, because per-taxon extraction reads them. {sample}_species_evidence.tsv, {sample}_report_gated.txt The k-mer evidence of every taxon at the Bracken rank, and the Kraken2 report without the taxa that fail it. Written on every run; Bracken reads the gated report only when shotgun.kmer_evidence.enabled is true. See species-level k-mer evidence.

The Kraken2 report has extra columns

MetaFlux runs Kraken2 with --report-minimizer-data, which inserts two minimizer-count columns into the report. The result has 8 columns rather than the standard 6, with rank, taxid and name pushed to the right. Anything that parses these reports by column position needs to know that — including the workflow's own read-tracking script, which reads rank from column 6.

docs.title: 03.abundance/
docs.text:
Bracken re-estimates abundance from the Kraken2 report at the rank set in shotgun.bracken.tax_lev, correcting the read counts that Kraken2 leaves stranded at higher ranks.

File Contents {sample}_report.txt The Bracken-corrected report, same layout as a Kraken2 report. Feeds the OTU table and MultiQC. Since v2.5.0 MetaFlux uses Bracken 3.1p1, bioconda's build of 3.1 with a fix for the report: plain 3.1 writes 0 in the third column (reads assigned directly to the taxon) on almost every row when tax_lev is not S. The second column, the clade count, is correct in both, and it is the only count MetaFlux uses. {sample}_output.txt Bracken's own per-taxon table for that sample. otu_table.biom Cross-sample abundance table in BIOM (HDF5) format. otu_table.tsv The same table as tab-separated text.

Rule finalize_otu_table builds both OTU tables straight from the per-sample Bracken reports, from the same rows and numbers, so they always agree. Each row is one taxon at tax_lev, each column one sample, and each value is the clade count of that taxon's row in the sample's Bracken report (0 where the sample does not have it). Each row carries a lineage of eight slots taken from the reports' own rank codes (see below). Rows come in the order the taxa are first met, reading the samples in the order of the table's columns, which are sorted by sample name (as in samples.tsv). The rule then applies the optional shotgun.taxonomy_filter keep/discard lists. In the BIOM file the sample metadata field Id holds the plain sample name.

docs.title: With shotgun.profiler: sylph or both
docs.text:
sylph writes its own files, next to the Kraken2 ones under both and instead of them under sylph. The two sets are never merged.

File Contents 03.abundance/sylph_table.tsv Read pairs per genome and sample, estimated from genome coverage, plus a last row unassigned. Each column adds up to trimmed in stats/read_tracking.txt, except by a few pairs per million in a sample sylph explains to 100 % (see Reading the numbers). 03.abundance/sylph_table.biom The same table in BIOM (HDF5) format. 03.abundance/sylph_table.genome_copies.tsv Each genome's share of genome copies (%) among the detected genomes; same rows, no unassigned. 03.abundance/sylph_genomes.tsv One row per genome: species name, whether it is a placeholder, the FASTA header of the reference genome, the placeholder-genus flag, best coverage and ANI. 03.abundance/sylph_profile.tsv sylph's own output, unchanged: one row per sample and genome. stats/sylph/sylph_summary.tsv One row per sample: read pairs after QC, the share the detected genomes explain, genomes found, flagged genomes. sylph_summary_mqc.tsv next to it is the copy MultiQC reads. 02.classification/sylph/ The sketches (sketches/{sample}.paired.sylsp, kept), sylph-tax's taxprof/{sample}.sylphmpa files, and sylph's own log lines for each sample.

How to read these numbers is explained on the sylph page.

docs.title: 04.extracted_reads/
docs.text: Only produced when shotgun.extract_taxa lists at least one taxon name. Files are {sample}_{taxon}_R1.fastq.gz and _R2, where {taxon} is the configured name lowercased with spaces turned into underscores — Escherichia coli becomes escherichia_coli. Reads assigned to that taxon and everything below it are pulled out of the classified reads. A taxon absent from a sample yields an empty pair of files rather than a failure. See per-taxon read extraction.

docs.title: stats/read_tracking.txt, samples.tsv and multiqc/
docs.text:
read_tracking.txt is one row per sample, one column per stage:

sample → raw → [nophix] → [no_host] → trimmed → classified → unclassified

nophix appears only when PhiX removal ran, no_host only when host removal ran. Every number is read pairs, not reads: BBDuk and fastp count the two mates separately and the script halves them, while Kraken2 already counts a pair once. classified and unclassified come from the Kraken2 report's root and unclassified rows. Under shotgun.profiler: sylph, Kraken2 does not run and the table ends at trimmed.

samples.tsv is a small manifest with the columns sample, source, bioproject, r1, r2 — handy for a downstream R or Python script that should not have to re-parse the config or re-glob the FASTQ directory. source is local or bioproject.

multiqc/multiqc_report.html collects fastp, Kraken2, Bracken and — when PhiX removal ran — the BBDuk statistics. BBMap host removal contributes nothing to the report; its counts are in stats/read_tracking.txt and its mapping rate in logs/decontam_host/{sample}.log. When sylph runs, the report also has a sylph table section, built from stats/sylph/sylph_summary_mqc.tsv; under profiler: sylph it has no Kraken2 or Bracken sections.

docs.title: Taxonomy strings in the final tables
docs.text:
Both modes write taxonomy the same way: ranks joined by ; with no space, each rank carrying its prefix. Which ranks a table has follows one rule, the same for every marker and every profiler:

  • d__ is always the domain slot and k__ always the kingdom slot. A table has a kingdom only where its reference defines one; MetaFlux never makes one up.
  • Kraken2 tables follow Kraken2's report codes: always eight slots, d__ k__ p__ c__ o__ f__ g__ s__, on any database.
  • Amplicon tables and sylph tables follow their reference files.
Output Slots Count 16S, SILVA 144 d__ k__ p__ c__ o__ f__ g__ s__ (s__ from addSpecies, so under method: rdp only) 8 16S, SILVA 138.2 d__ p__ c__ o__ f__ g__ s__ 7 ITS, UNITE k__ p__ c__ o__ f__ g__ s__ (UNITE has no domain) 7 18S, PR2, method: rdp d__ sg__ dv__ sbd__ c__ o__ f__ g__ s__ 9 18S, PR2, method: sintax d__ sg__ dv__ c__ o__ f__ g__ s__ (dv__ holds Division and Subdivision joined by -) 8 gyrB, DD7RZ8 the gene tag (gyrB or other, no prefix), then p__ c__ o__ f__ g__ s__ 7 rpoB, FROGS d__ p__ c__ o__ f__ g__ s__ 7 Kraken2 (otu_table), any database d__ k__ p__ c__ o__ f__ g__ s__ (k__ empty on a GTDB database, which has no kingdom rank, and for taxa without a kingdom, most protists among them) 8 sylph (sylph_table) d__ p__ c__ o__ f__ g__ s__ (GTDB has no kingdom) 7

In the amplicon tables, ranks the classifier could not resolve are simply left out, so a string can end early (d__Bacteria;k__Pseudomonadati;p__Pseudomonadota). The shotgun tables always write every slot and leave empty any slot they have no name for, and every slot below shotgun.bracken.tax_lev (…;g__Bacteroides;s__ in a genus-level table).

Values in d__ that are not domains. Three kinds:

  • A virus realm, in the Kraken2 table. A virus has no domain. ICTV, which names virus taxa, made the realm the top rank of virus taxonomy, in place of the domain, and NCBI keeps domains and realms in one field of its taxonomy, so the realm sits where a cellular organism's domain sits, with the viral kingdom in k__: d__Duplodnaviria;k__Heunggongvirae;p__Uroviricota;c__Caudoviricetes;o__;f__Peduoviridae;g__Peduovirus;s__Peduovirus P37. A virus that NCBI places in no realm keeps an empty d__, and so does anything else without a domain, plasmids for example. Realm names follow the NCBI taxonomy the database was built with. d__Viruses never appears, also on a database built when NCBI still ranked Viruses a superkingdom.
  • d__Unassigned, on the unassigned row of the sylph table.
  • PR2's organelle tags, in 18S tables: d__Eukaryota:plas (plastid), :mito, :nucl (nucleomorph), :apic (apicoplast) and :chro (chromatophore).

k__ in ITS tables holds whatever UNITE files at its top rank: kingdoms (k__Fungi, k__Viridiplantae, k__Metazoa), protist groups (k__Alveolata, k__Stramenopila, k__Rhizaria, …) and placeholders (k__Protista, k__unidentified, k__Eukaryota_kgd_Incertae_sedis).

With shotgun.profiler: both the same organism reads differently in the two tables: otu_table.tsv has eight slots and sylph_table.tsv seven, and the two databases can name a taxon differently. Methanobrevibacter smithii in the D6331 run SRR38976715 (BioProject PRJNA1474435; see Benchmark data), as Kraken2 names it with PlusPF k2_pluspf_20260626 and as sylph names it with GTDB r232:

otu_table.tsv    d__Archaea;k__Methanobacteriati;p__Methanobacteriota;c__Methanobacteria;o__Methanobacteriales;f__Methanobacteriaceae;g__Methanobrevibacter;s__Methanobrevibacter smithii
sylph_table.tsv  d__Archaea;p__Methanobacteriota;c__Methanobacteria;o__Methanobacteriales;f__Methanobacteriaceae;g__Methanocatella;s__Methanocatella smithii

No MetaFlux step joins the two tables. Compare them by rank name, not by column position.

Other tools may write the same lineage another way: kraken-biom and MetaPhlAn, for example, put the domain under k__ (k__Bacteria). Filter tokens and scripts written for their tables need the d__ prefix in MetaFlux's.

With SILVA 144 and silva_other: verbatim (the default) a 16S rank name can end in --other (g__Bradyrhizobium--other); the species slot is still written with the plain genus (g__Lactobacillus--other;s__Lactobacillus iners). The kingdom never carries the suffix. See 16S rRNA.

The exact form of the species slot follows the reference database, not the pipeline:

Source Species slot Example 16S, SILVA via rdp (addSpecies) s__Genus species (a binomial, space-separated) s__Bacillus subtilis 16S via sintax none: SILVA's SINTAX file stops at genus — ITS, UNITE, both methods UNITE's own s__Genus_species (underscore) s__Agaricus_bisporus 18S, PR2 PR2's own s__Genus_species s__Unruhdinium_kevei gyrB (DD7RZ8), rpoB (FROGS) the reference's own s__Genus_species s__Staphylococcus_simiae Shotgun otu_table the whole species name, as the Kraken2 database writes it s__Escherichia coli, s__Peduovirus P37, s__uncultured Martelella sp. Shotgun sylph_table the GTDB species name exactly as GTDB writes it, placeholders included s__Escherichia coli_E, s__JABGUH01 sp018646675

In the amplicon tables the binomial is only assembled when the reference hands back a bare, lowercase epithet (subtilis, from addSpecies; or, under rdp, the epithet that DADA2 cuts out of UNITE's species, see ITS). A reference that already returns a complete name — PR2's Unruhdinium_kevei, for instance — is passed through untouched, so the genus is never glued on twice.

This happens in the taxonomy string only. In taxon_seq_table.txt, the Species column of 16S under rdp holds addSpecies' bare epithet (subtilis), and the binomial is only in the string; Reading the tables in R shows how to build it from the table. For every other marker and method the Species cell holds the same name as the s__ slot.

In the sylph table, a lineage table that writes the domain as k__ (FungiRefSeq's k__Eukaryota) is rewritten to d__, so every row uses the same seven prefixes. See sylph.

docs.title: Reading the tables in R
docs.text:
The tables follow the ranks of their reference (above), so one rank can sit in a different column from one marker, release or profiler to the next: tax[, 2] is the kingdom on SILVA 144 and the phylum on SILVA 138.2. Pick ranks by name, tax[, "Phylum"], which is the same column in every table that has a phylum.

Amplicon tables. taxon_seq_table.txt has one column per rank, already named after it, so it is the taxonomy table to hand to phyloseq, mia or any other package; there is no need to parse the taxonomy strings. A rank column with no value in any row comes into R as logical rather than as text, because read.table sees only NA in it; Species on 16S under sintax is always such a column. colClasses = "character" reads every column as text:

tax <- read.table("06.taxonomy/taxon_seq_table.txt", sep = "\t", header = TRUE,
                  row.names = 1, colClasses = "character")
tax[, "Phylum"]

On 16S under rdp, Species holds only the epithet (subtilis). This line writes the binomial of the taxonomy string into it, after dropping a trailing --other from the genus (SILVA 144 with silva_other: verbatim, the default). Run it on 16S rdp tables only: in the other tables the cell already holds the whole name.

tax[, "Species"] <- ifelse(is.na(tax[, "Species"]), NA,
                           paste(sub("--other$", "", tax[, "Genus"]), tax[, "Species"]))

Do not parse the taxonomy strings with phyloseq's parse_taxonomy_greengenes. It knows only the one-letter prefixes k__ to s__, so it names the d__ column Rank1, and it misreads the longer 18S prefixes: sg__TSAR comes out as a column named Species holding sTSAR.

Shotgun BIOM files (otu_table.biom, sylph_table.biom):

  • phyloseq's import_biom() with parse_taxonomy_greengenes names the first column Rank1, for the same reason; rename it:

    library(phyloseq)
ps <- import_biom("03.abundance/otu_table.biom",
                  parseFunction = parse_taxonomy_greengenes)
colnames(tax_table(ps))[1] <- "Domain"

  • mia names the columns after the prefixes itself (domain, kingdom, phylum, …) when asked to:

    tse <- mia::importBIOM("03.abundance/otu_table.biom",
                       rank.from.prefix = TRUE, prefix.rm = TRUE)

  • ampvis2 accepts a Domain or a Kingdom column, but stops with "Cannot have both Domain and Kingdom columns at the same time in taxonomy." on a table that has both, as every Kraken2 table and every 16S table on SILVA 144 does. Drop one of the two columns before loading.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Configuration — the keys referred to above.
  • Running MetaFlux — what a re-run rebuilds, and what it leaves alone.
  • Troubleshooting — what an empty or collapsing table usually means.

docs.title: Running MetaFlux
docs.text: MetaFlux is launched with snakemake. Everything that varies between runs lives in the config file, so the command line stays short and looks the same for both modes.

docs.title: Run from the repository root
docs.text:
The Snakefile resolves configfile: "config/config.yaml" against the directory the command was launched from, not against its own location. Two more lookups behave the same way: references.refdb_root defaults to the relative path refdb, and user-supplied marker packs are read from config/markers/. Launching from somewhere else silently changes where all three point.

Paths inside the config (input.fastq_dir, output.out_dir, references.kraken_db, the primer FASTAs) are best given as absolute paths, which makes them immune to this.

docs.title: The two commands
docs.text:
# Always preview the plan first
snakemake --sdm conda --cores 16 --configfile config/config.yaml --dry-run

# Execute
snakemake --sdm conda --cores 16 --configfile config/config.yaml

A dry run (--dry-run, or -n) builds the job list and prints it without running anything or writing any file. Do one before every run: MetaFlux does most of its checks while the workflow is read, before any job starts. A dry run therefore catches, among others:

  • mode set to something other than amplicon or shotgun;
  • an amplicon.type that matches no marker pack;
  • primer FASTAs that do not exist (amplicon), or a kraken_db that does not exist (shotgun);
  • a config still using the retired include_pattern / exclude_pattern filter keys;
  • a keep/discard token that can never match the run's taxonomy strings, such as k__Bacteria from a config written for MetaFlux v2.4.0 or earlier (now d__Bacteria);
  • a marker pack in config/markers/ written for an older MetaFlux;
  • ITS combined with length_filter.mode: auto but a manual expected_length, which would otherwise crash after the full DADA2 run.

While reading the workflow, MetaFlux also prints a banner line to stderr:

[MetaFlux v2.5.0] mode=amplicon, input=local, 24 sample(s) in /data/fastq

Before it, an amplicon run prints a line saying whether the organelle filter is on, and a 16S run one more naming the SILVA release in use — the quickest check that references.silva.release and amplicon.taxonomy.silva_other were picked up:

[MetaFlux] organelle filter: on — ASVs that Metaxa2 calls mitochondria or chloroplast are removed
[MetaFlux] 16S reference: SILVA 144 (silva_other: verbatim; trainset silva_nr99_v144_toGenus_7rank_other-verbatim_trainset.fa.gz)

Checking that the sample count is the expected one costs nothing and catches a mistyped fastq_dir or a mate-naming mismatch before a long run starts.

--configfile is optional

The Snakefile already loads config/config.yaml. Passing --configfile makes the choice explicit, and is how a different config — one per marker, or one per project — is selected.

docs.title: --sdm conda and --conda-prefix
docs.text:
--sdm conda is short for --software-deployment-method conda. It tells Snakemake to build each rule's own conda environment from the YAML files in workflow/envs/ and to run that rule inside it. Only Snakemake itself has to be installed by hand; DADA2, Cutadapt, Kraken2, Bracken and the rest are installed by the workflow on first use. Leaving the flag out makes every rule run against whatever happens to be on PATH, which is exactly what the per-rule environments exist to avoid.

The environments are built once and then reused. By default they go into .snakemake/conda/ inside the working directory, which is why running from the repository root keeps reusing the same ones. --conda-prefix moves them somewhere else:

snakemake --sdm conda --conda-prefix ~/.metaflux-envs --cores 16

That is useful when several checkouts, several users, or several working directories should share one set of environments instead of each building its own — they are a few gigabytes in total, and building them takes minutes.

Pre-build the environments

--conda-create-envs-only builds every environment and stops. Handy before a cluster run, so the compute nodes are not each waiting on conda, and on machines where the network is only reachable from the login node.

docs.title: Useful patterns
docs.text:
# Override the mode without editing the config
snakemake --sdm conda --cores 16 --config mode=shotgun

# Cap concurrent memory (e.g. memory-bound steps)
snakemake --sdm conda --cores 16 --resources mem_mb=32000

# Resume after an interruption
snakemake --sdm conda --cores 16 --rerun-incomplete

# Cluster execution: supply a profile (e.g. SLURM) — per-rule threads/mem_mb are honoured
snakemake --sdm conda --profile <slurm-profile>

Overriding the mode. --config mode=shotgun replaces the top-level mode key for that invocation only; the file on disk is untouched and every other setting still comes from it. The shotgun section of the config has to be filled in for this to work — references.kraken_db in particular, which is checked while the workflow is read. Nested settings (amplicon.type, for instance) can't be reached with a dotted key — --config only accepts plain top-level identifiers, so overriding one means replacing its whole parent block with inline YAML (--config 'amplicon={type: ITS}') rather than a single key=value pair. Keeping one config file per marker and selecting it with --configfile is clearer.

Give each mode its own out_dir

Both modes write stats/read_tracking.txt and multiqc/multiqc_report.html. Running the second mode into the first mode's output directory overwrites them. The same applies to running two markers into one directory: the ASV files in 05.dada2/ are not named after the marker.

Limiting concurrency. --cores is the total CPU budget on the machine; a rule asking for more threads than that is scaled down to fit. Lowering --cores is therefore the way to run fewer heavy jobs side by side. Memory is capped separately: every heavy rule declares a mem_mb — from resources.mem_mb.* in the config, except Kraken2 and sylph_profile, whose figures are computed while the workflow is read — so --resources mem_mb=32000 lets Snakemake start jobs only while their declared memory still fits in 32 GB. This matters most for Kraken2 with shotgun.kraken.memory_mapping: false, where every concurrent process loads its own full copy of the database, and for the DADA2 steps, which hold all samples in memory at once.

--jobs is not a second lever here. On a local run Snakemake treats it as an alias for --cores, and passing both switches the core budget off rather than adding a job cap on top of it — --jobs 4 --cores 16 would run four jobs at once whatever their thread counts add up to. It belongs on cluster runs only, see below.

Resuming. An interrupted run leaves two kinds of debris. Files that a job was part-way through writing are marked incomplete, and --rerun-incomplete rebuilds them instead of trusting them. A run killed outright (Ctrl-C twice, a node failure, an OOM kill) can also leave the working directory locked, which Snakemake reports on the next launch; snakemake --unlock clears it. Everything that finished cleanly is kept and not recomputed.

Cluster execution. A profile holds the submission settings for the scheduler (partition, account, how threads and mem_mb map to sbatch arguments), so the MetaFlux command line does not change. The per-rule values come from resources.threads.<rule> and resources.mem_mb.<rule> in the config, falling back to threads_default (4) and mem_mb_default (2000) for any rule not listed. Kraken2 is the exception: its memory request is computed while the workflow is read, from shotgun.kraken.memory_mapping and the actual size of the database's hash.k2d — 20000 MB with memory mapping on (the database itself is shared through the operating system's file cache), otherwise the hash size plus 10 % headroom. With a profile, --jobs becomes the cap on jobs queued with the scheduler at once — the one setting where it does something --cores does not.

docs.title: What happens on a re-run
docs.text:
Snakemake only rebuilds what is missing or out of date. Re-running a completed workflow with no changes does nothing at all and says so. Three practical consequences:

  • A deleted or edited output is rebuilt, and only what is needed to rebuild it runs. Deleting 06.taxonomy/asv_table.txt re-runs assign_taxonomy; the DADA2 steps upstream are already satisfied and are skipped.
  • Changing the config can be enough to mark a step out of date. Current Snakemake versions consider more than file timestamps: a changed rule parameter, a changed script, or a changed conda environment also count. Because the contaminant keep/discard lists reach assign_taxonomy as rule parameters, editing them re-runs the taxonomy step alone and leaves the denoising untouched. Adding --rerun-triggers mtime restricts the comparison to timestamps only.
  • A dry run shows what would run. -n prints the jobs a re-run would execute.

Re-running an output folder made with v2.4.0

Every step runs again. The output folders have new names: the amplicon folders 1.reads to 7.phylogeny are now 01.reads to 07.phylogeny, and the read-count files in stats/ take the same two digits (01.raw_reads.counts …); in shotgun mode the Kraken2 files move from 02.classification/ into 02.classification/kraken2/, together with the k-mer evidence files of 02b.evidence/. The few steps whose files kept their names run again too, because MetaFlux now ships a pin file next to every conda environment (the exact package builds it was tested with; see Installation) and Snakemake counts that file as part of the software a step ran with: the QC of the raw reads in stats/, the primer reverse complements in _aux/, the reference files already in refdb/ (downloaded and built again, same content) and, in BioProject mode, the download of the SRA runs. Only samples.tsv is kept, the one step without a conda environment whose file kept its name. To keep the SRA runs and the reference files already on disk, start the run once with --rerun-triggers mtime params input code: it leaves the software-environment trigger out, and everything that moved runs again anyway. The old folders and count files, the old files directly in 02.classification/, and 03.abundance/otu_table.raw.biom (v2.4.0's intermediate table, which a run made with --notemp keeps) are left as they are and can be deleted.

Results that change on purpose:

  • Taxonomy strings: d__ is always the domain slot and k__ the kingdom slot (see taxonomy strings). 16S moves to SILVA 144, the new default: d__Bacteria;k__Pseudomonadati;p__…. On SILVA 138.2 (references: {silva: {release: "138.2"}}, the release v2.4.0 used) and on rpoB: d__Bacteria;p__…. ITS, 18S and gyrB keep their ranks. The shotgun otu_table has eight slots on every Kraken2 database, a virus carries its realm in d__, species names are whole, and in otu_table.biom the sample Id is the plain sample name (it was <sample>_report).
  • 16S on SILVA 138.2: the length probe now leaves chloroplast, mitochondrial and eukaryote references out. For 799F/1175R, 515F/806R and 341F/805R the probe's p95 does not change, so neither do truncLen and the denoised ASVs and counts; the auto ASV length window can move by a base (for 799F/1175R, the primers of the 16S test dataset, its lower edge moves from 324 to 325 bp).
  • 18S with sintax: almost every ASV whose taxonomy was empty now carries its domain, nearly always d__Eukaryota (158 of 159 on the 18S test dataset).
  • ITS with rdp: the species reads Genus_epithet, as with sintax. All taxonomy tables have one format under both methods ("" as first header cell, NA for a rank not reached), and the rank cells of taxon_seq_table.txt hold bare names.
  • The taxon filter can remove more organelle ASVs (best-hit check, organelle filter). A lineage near the cutoff can gain or lose a rank (VSEARCH 2.32 under sintax; under rdp, as between two identical runs), so an ASV at the cutoff of a keep token's rank can be kept by one version and removed by the other.
  • Shotgun: Kraken2 2.17.1, Bracken 3.1p1 and bbmap 39.52 are pinned, so a folder made with other releases can get slightly different results; at a tax_lev other than S the OTU table is now built correctly (see Troubleshooting); nophix in the read tracking now counts exactly the read pairs BBDuk kept, so raw minus nophix is the pairs it removed (a pair with PhiX in one mate only used to count as half a pair).

Stops at start-up: a filter token such as k__Bacteria (the message names the one to write, d__Bacteria); a shotgun.bracken.tax_lev other than P, C, O, F, G or S (such as D or K); a marker pack in config/markers/ written for an older MetaFlux (copy the shipped pack again and re-apply your change). See Troubleshooting.

Reference files: the SILVA 144 files are downloaded and built once, and the 18S PR2 SINTAX file is built once (neither existed in v2.4.0); the rpoB reference is built again under a new name (the FROGS rpoB archive is downloaded again); the SILVA 138.2 SINTAX file is rebuilt under its old name, with the same content, so a refdb folder shared with a v2.4.0 checkout keeps working for both.

Two caches deliberately sit outside this machinery and survive across runs: reference databases under refdb/, and the amplicon-length probe result under refdb/cache/ inside the MetaFlux checkout — that second path is fixed and does not follow references.refdb_root. The probe's filename encodes the marker, its reference (for 16S also the lineages left out of the statistics; for rpoB _excl-second-site, because products that hold a second forward-primer site are left out), and a hash of both primer sequences, so it is reused whenever those are unchanged and recomputed when a primer changes. See output files for what a run writes where.

docs.title: Two mode-specific notes
docs.text:
Shotgun, BioProject mode

Setting input.bioproject to an NCBI accession makes MetaFlux resolve the project's PAIRED runs through NCBI e-utils and download them into fastq_dir before anything else. Single-end runs are skipped — they do not fit the rest of the pipeline. The run list is cached as {accession}_runinfo.csv in fastq_dir, so later invocations do not need the network for that step, and input.accession_list narrows the set to named runs.

Shotgun, first Kraken2 call

The first Kraken2 job reads the whole database off disk. That is slow while the cache is cold and fast once the operating system has the database in memory, so a first sample that seems to hang is usually just loading.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Configuration — every key referred to here.
  • Output files — what the run produces and which file feeds which step.
  • Troubleshooting — YAML errors, empty tables, and the truncLen trap.

docs.title: Choosing confidence and threshold
docs.text:
Two Kraken2/Bracken settings affect how many false species calls reach the final table: the Kraken2 confidence score and the Bracken read threshold. In the benchmark on this page, changing confidence had little effect on accuracy. The threshold had the largest effect of any shotgun setting tested, and a fixed value suits only one sequencing depth: at Bracken's default of 10, accuracy fell the more deeply a sample was sequenced.

  • shotgun.kraken.confidence — leave it at 0.15.
  • shotgun.bracken.threshold — set it to auto (the default).

This page is the benchmark behind that recommendation: what was tested, how, and what it did and did not show. If you only want the setting, skip to The recommendation.

docs.title: Effect on a mock community
docs.text:
Kraken2 classifies a read to the taxon its k-mers best match, however thin that match is. Bracken then re-estimates abundance from those calls. Neither step, by default, asks how much evidence a taxon actually has before trusting it — Bracken's own floor (-t, ten reads) has been ten reads since its first release, at any sequencing depth.

Species-level results on a mock community of known composition, the ZymoBIOMICS Gut Microbiome Standard (D6331), SRA run SRR38976715 (BioProject PRJNA1474435), classified with PlusPF k2_pluspf_20260626 at Kraken2 confidence 0.15, the v2.5.0 defaults:

Species scored Precision Recall F1 Bracken's default, -t 10 53 0.283 0.882 0.429 MetaFlux default, threshold: auto (-t 265) 19 0.737 0.824 0.778

The mock's Fusobacterium, listed by Zymo as F. nucleatum, is scored as F. animalis, so calls of F. nucleatum, F. polymorphum and F. vincentii count as false positives. Bracken also reports Homo sapiens at both thresholds: human DNA in the sample, not part of the standard, so it is left out of the scores. Benchmark data gives the reasons for both.

Recall fell slightly, from 0.88 to 0.82: Salmonella enterica, with 135 Kraken2 reads, fell below the threshold. Precision rose from 0.28 to 0.74. At -t 10, 38 of the 53 species scored were not in the mock. Bracken reports a species only when Kraken2 gave it at least -t reads, so each of them had at least ten Kraken2 reads. Most of them (29 of the 38) are in the same genus as a member of the mock and share conserved regions with it; database cross-contamination is another source. The five false species left at -t 265 are all Fusobacterium species closely related to the mock's F. animalis.

docs.title: Kraken2 confidence — keep it at 0.15
docs.text:
Raising the confidence score removes far fewer weakly supported species than the Bracken threshold does, because Kraken2 does not reject a read that falls short of the confidence threshold: it moves the call up the taxonomy tree until the score clears the bar, and only reports "unclassified" if even the root fails. Raising confidence therefore mostly moves reads to coarser ranks, which leaves more reads for Bracken to redistribute.

The measured consequence: raising confidence lowers the read count of species-level calls, and a rare species can lose a large share of its few reads. On the same D6331 reads, Salmonella enterica, 0.01 % of the mock's DNA, had 135 Kraken2 reads at confidence 0.15 and 85 at 0.20 (PlusPF k2_pluspf_20260626; 134 and 87 with k2_pluspf_20251015).

Raising confidence and applying a read-count floor both reduce the same small read counts, so together they remove rare species that are present. Wright, Comeau & Langille (2023) swept confidence 0.00–1.00 on simulated data: 0.60 gave the highest mean F1, while 0.15 gave the lowest L1 distance, that is, the most accurate relative abundances. 0.15 is the source of MetaFlux's default, and nothing here changes it.

docs.title: Why a fixed number is wrong
docs.text:
The right floor depends on how many reads a sample has. A species with 200 reads is better supported in a sample of 2 million classified read pairs than in one of 15 million: auto sets -t 100 in the first, which keeps it, and -t 750 in the second, which removes it. A fixed threshold is therefore right for one depth only. In the first benchmark behind the default, with PlusPF k2_pluspf_20251015, one CAMI II marine sample (sample 0) was subsampled to 2, 5 and 10 million read pairs and also used at its full 16.6 million. At Bracken's default of 10, F1 was lower the deeper the sample was sequenced:

classified pairs F1 at fixed -t 10 1.8 M 0.740 4.5 M 0.667 9.0 M 0.612 15.0 M 0.576

With the community and all other settings unchanged, F1 fell from 0.740 to 0.576 (22 %) as depth increased. A depth-scaled threshold over the same range stayed at 0.82–0.83.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
threshold = max(threshold_min, threshold_alpha × classified_read_pairs)

Units matter: classified read pairs, not raw reads, not trimmed reads. Kraken2 in paired mode counts a pair as one unit, and the classified fraction depends on how well the database covers the community: with PlusPF k2_pluspf_20260626, 99.8 % of the D6331 mock's read pairs were classified, against 47–75 % for the four wastewater metagenomes of the shotgun test dataset, at similar depth (5.3 million read pairs entering Kraken2 for the mock, 3.5–4.7 million for the wastewater metagenomes). Raw input reads would therefore be the wrong denominator.

shotgun:
  bracken:
    threshold: auto            # or a fixed integer
    threshold_alpha: 5.0e-05
    threshold_min: 10

With auto, MetaFlux reads the classified-pair count from Kraken2's own report after it finishes — the count does not exist until then — and computes the threshold per sample. The decision is written to that sample's Bracken log; for the D6331 run it reads:

[bracken] auto threshold: 5e-05 x 5292994 classified read pairs -> -t 265

docs.title: Where alpha comes from, and what is and is not new here
docs.text:
-t is Bracken's own parameter, and Bracken does not scale it: it takes a flat integer and does nothing else with it. A cut-off that grows with depth is not a new idea. Benchmarks usually filter on relative abundance, a fixed share of the reads (for example Ye et al. 2019), and KrakenUniq found that the best unique-k-mer threshold rose roughly linearly with sequencing depth (Breitwieser et al. 2018).

MetaFlux adds a measured constant and computes the threshold for each sample automatically:

  • a depth exponent of 0.967, fitted in the first benchmark on one CAMI II marine sample classified at four depths (1.8 to 15 million classified pairs, the series above), consistent with a threshold directly proportional to depth
  • a coefficient, alpha = 5×10⁻⁵, chosen in the first benchmark (PlusPF k2_pluspf_20251015) and re-fitted on all 41 CAMI II samples with k2_pluspf_20260626, where the median optimum was 6.0×10⁻⁵; on the D6331 mock the optimum is several times higher (next section)
  • the auto computation itself, run per sample inside the bracken rule

None of this is standard terminology. "Alpha" is the name given here to the proportionality constant; if you cite this elsewhere, describe it as a depth-scaled Bracken threshold with a benchmark-fitted coefficient, not as a published Bracken feature.

docs.title: How firmly alpha is established
docs.text:
Community (samples) Species per sample Optimal alpha ZymoBIOMICS D6331, run SRR38976715 17 2.3×10⁻⁴ – 3.5×10⁻⁴ CAMI II strain-madness, samples 0–9 20 4.1×10⁻⁵ – 1.2×10⁻⁴ CAMI II marine, samples 0–9 256–381 5.2×10⁻⁵ – 2.1×10⁻⁴ CAMI II rhizosphere, samples 0–20 73–126 1.5×10⁻⁵ – 2.6×10⁻⁴

The optimal alpha is the -t with the highest species F1, divided by the sample's classified read pairs. D6331: the run in Effect on a mock community (PlusPF k2_pluspf_20260626, confidence 0.15), where F1 reaches 0.903 for any -t from 1,191 to 1,832. CAMI II rows: the range of the per-sample optima in the 41-sample re-fit with PlusPF k2_pluspf_20260626.

Pooling the 41 CAMI II samples gives a median optimal alpha of 6.0×10⁻⁵, 1.2× the default. One constant works for these samples despite the spread because F1 changes little over a wide range of alpha: using 5×10⁻⁵ everywhere costs a mean of 0.023 F1 against tuning each sample to its own best (median cost 0.014). In the first benchmark, Bracken's default of 10 cost up to 0.34 F1.

The D6331 mock is an exception: there the default costs 0.125 F1 against the optimum (0.778 against 0.903).

Adjusting alpha for a known community

A smaller threshold_alpha is a looser filter, a larger one a stricter filter. The best value differs between communities and between samples of one community (table above), and it does not follow the number of species: the optimum of the 17-species D6331 mock is 4.5 to 7 times the default, while the optima of the 20-species strain-madness samples range from 0.8 to 2.4 times it. The default is recommended for routine use.

docs.title: The recommendation
docs.text:
shotgun:
  kraken:
    confidence: 0.15            # unchanged; do not raise it alongside the threshold
  bracken:
    threshold: auto
    threshold_alpha: 5.0e-05
    threshold_min: 10

Worked examples: 2M classified pairs → -t ≈ 100 · 5M → ≈ 250 · 15M → ≈ 750.

docs.title: What this does — and does not — fix
docs.text:
The threshold raises precision substantially, lowers recall slightly and changes abundance accuracy little.

On the D6331 run, the L1 distance between the Bracken profile and the genomic-DNA composition in Zymo's manual (the sum of absolute differences, in percentage points) was 40.86 at both -t 10 and -t 265, and the Bray–Curtis dissimilarity between the two profiles was 0.0009. The threshold changes which taxa are named, not how much of each is reported. If your downstream work is ordination or differential abundance on already-good tables, expect little change. If it is species counts, richness, or presence/absence, expect a large one.

It cannot rescue a database that does not cover your community. Only 165 of the 307 true species of the CAMI II rhizosphere (plant-associated) set, samples 0–20, are in PlusPF at all: 54 % over the whole set and 42 % per sample on average, the same in k2_pluspf_20251015 and k2_pluspf_20260626. No parameter setting recovers the rest, and species F1 stays near 0.3 at every setting tested. The gap lies in the reference database, and a database update alone should not be expected to close it.

docs.title: The benchmark behind these numbers
docs.text:
Real data with known composition: the ZymoBIOMICS Gut Microbiome Standard (D6331), SRA run SRR38976715 (BioProject PRJNA1474435; see Benchmark data), 17 species after strain-collapse, with its Fusobacterium scored as F. animalis; classified with PlusPF k2_pluspf_20251015 and k2_pluspf_20260626.

Simulated data with gold-standard truth: CAMI II marine samples 0–9, rhizosphere (plant-associated) samples 0–20 and strain-madness samples 0–9 (every strain-madness sample holds the same 20 species by design), 41 samples in all. All 41 were classified with PlusPF k2_pluspf_20260626; five of them were also classified with k2_pluspf_20251015 for the first choice of alpha.

Real data with no known composition: the four wastewater metagenomes of the shotgun test dataset (BioProject PRJNA1477390, runs SRR39106521–SRR39106524). Without a truth table they give no accuracy figures; this page uses them for the classified fractions under The rule, and What it does on real data shows the k-mer evidence gate on them.

Scorer check: the benchmark scorer was checked against OPAL 1.0.13, the CAMI assessment tool, on the Bracken species tables of the two runs with PlusPF k2_pluspf_20260626 (Kraken2 confidence 0.15 and 0.20), which cover the 41 CAMI II samples and the D6331 mock. With its inputs prepared as the scorer prepares them, OPAL's species-level true positives, false positives and false negatives equal the scorer's in every sample. Run on the gold standards as distributed, OPAL differs only in the taxa those preparation rules touch: gold taxids that NCBI has merged since the CAMI release, placeholder names such as "uncultured bacterium", which the scorer does not score, and F. animalis, which the scorer counted as the mock's F. nucleatum in this check; the D6331 figures on this page score F. animalis as the true member instead. The first benchmark, the 41-sample re-fit behind the CAMI II rows of the alpha table and the k2_pluspf_20251015 runs were not part of this check.

Comparator: MetaPhlAn 4, database mpa_vJan26_CHOCOPhlAnSGB_202605, on the same trimmed reads of the D6331 run. MetaPhlAn reported 14 of the 17 species and no false ones (F1 0.90). MetaFlux at its v2.5.0 defaults (PlusPF k2_pluspf_20260626) reported the same 14 species and five false ones, all of them Fusobacterium species related to the mock's F. animalis (F1 0.78). MetaFlux also reported Homo sapiens, from human DNA in the sample; it is not scored, and MetaPhlAn, whose database holds only microbial markers, cannot report it.

docs.text:

docs.title: Reference databases (shotgun)
docs.text:
Amplicon mode fetches its reference databases on first use and caches them under refdb/. Shotgun mode does not: the Kraken2 database is large, version-sensitive, and usually shared between projects on a machine, so it is supplied rather than downloaded by the workflow.

Reference Provisioning Config key Kraken2 / Bracken index user-supplied, required when Kraken2 runs (shotgun.profiler: kraken2, the default, or both) references.kraken_db sylph databases + lineage tables user-supplied, only with shotgun.profiler: sylph or both — see sylph references.sylph_databases, references.sylph_taxonomy_dir Host genome(s) user-supplied, optional shotgun.decontamination.host_genomes PhiX bundled inside the BBTools package — nothing to fetch (none)

PhiX is worth a note: the references.phix block in the config is used by amplicon mode, which downloads the genome and builds a bowtie2 index from it. Shotgun mode uses BBDuk's own bundled phix2.fa.gz instead, so no shotgun rule uses that block. Keep it anyway: references.phix.fasta is read at start-up, in both modes.

docs.title: Pointing MetaFlux at the database
docs.text:
references:
  kraken_db: /path/to/db/k2_pluspf      # [shotgun] — user-supplied

When Kraken2 runs (shotgun.profiler: kraken2, the default, or both), the path is checked at start-up, before any job runs. A missing or mistyped path then stops the run immediately with:

[MetaFlux] mode=shotgun requires kraken_db but not found: /path/to/db/k2_pluspf

The key points at the directory, not at a file. A Kraken2 database directory holds:

File Used by What it is hash.k2d Kraken2 the k-mer → taxon hash — by far the largest file, and the one that sets the memory requirement opts.k2d Kraken2 the options the index was built with taxo.k2d Kraken2, and MetaFlux when the run starts the taxonomy tree *.kmer_distrib Bracken per-read-length k-mer distributions, one file per supported read length

Bracken is pointed at the same directory, which is why the .kmer_distrib files must be present alongside the index. Pre-built downloads from the catalog below include them.

MetaFlux reads taxo.k2d itself too, once, when the run starts. It is Kraken2's own copy of the database taxonomy, written when the index is built and read at every classification, so every Kraken2 database has it. From it MetaFlux takes which taxa the database ranks as a domain, a kingdom or a virus realm. The OTU table needs that: its lineage has eight fixed slots, d__ k__ p__ c__ o__ f__ g__ s__, filled from the rank codes of the Bracken reports, but Kraken2 has no code for a virus realm (on current databases it prints a realm as an unranked R2 row, like other unranked nodes), and the domain and kingdom codes of the reports are checked against the database (see OTU table). A directory without a readable taxo.k2d stops the run at start-up:

[MetaFlux] /path/to/db/k2_pluspf/taxo.k2d not found: references.kraken_db must be a complete Kraken2 database (hash.k2d, opts.k2d and taxo.k2d).

What the database's taxonomy has shows in the table. A GTDB database has domains but no kingdom rank and no viruses, so k__ stays empty in every row; an NCBI database fills k__ for most bacteria and archaea, the fungi, plants and animals, but not for most protists, which NCBI places in no kingdom. Realm names follow the NCBI taxonomy the database was built with.

docs.title: Choosing an index
docs.text:
Pre-built indexes — with sizes, build dates and md5 checksums — are listed in Ben Langmead's catalog. A standard choice is PlusPF — the Standard collection with protozoa and fungi added — at roughly 100 GB for the full build.

The same collections are also published as size-capped builds — pluspf_16gb, for example — which are reduced to fit a memory ceiling, and much larger ones such as core_nt exist at the other end. All of them work. With memory_mapping: false, MetaFlux reads the index size from disk and sizes its memory request accordingly; with memory mapping on — the shipped default — it requests a fixed 20 GB of private workspace and lets the kernel page the index in, so the size on disk is not consulted at all. See Memory.

The choice affects the results as well as the memory needed. A capped index holds fewer k-mers, so more reads go unclassified and species-level calls become less reliable; with a shallow index, re-estimating at genus level with shotgun.bracken.tax_lev: G is often the more reliable choice.

Two practical rules when choosing:

  • The database defines what can be found. Fungi and protozoa are absent from the Standard collection, so a soil or gut study that expects them needs PlusPF or wider.
  • Record the exact dated build. Two runs against different builds of "PlusPF" are not comparable, and the build date is what belongs in a methods section.

A missing organism does not show up as unclassified

The unclassified fraction shows only part of what the database is missing.

When an organism is absent from the index but a relative is present, its reads do not fail to classify. Their k-mers genuinely occur in that relative, so they map to it, the lowest common ancestor resolves within that relative's lineage, and the confidence score is high — because agreement with the assigned clade really is high. The result is a confident species-level call for an organism that was never in the sample.

Raising confidence does not help here. The score measures how much of a read's evidence supports the taxon it was given, and nothing in that calculation can distinguish "this read is from X" from "this read is from an unsequenced relative of X". So a low unclassified fraction shows neither that the database was adequate nor that the species calls are right.

The practical defences are to use an index that covers the expected community, to re-estimate at genus level where species representation is thin (shotgun.bracken.tax_lev: G), and to treat species-level calls from a sparse index as hypotheses rather than identifications.

docs.title: Kraken2 version
docs.text:
MetaFlux runs one Kraken2 release, 2.17.1. It is pinned in the environment file workflow/envs/kraken2.yaml, so every install runs the same Kraken2; report it together with the dated build of the index. Kraken2 2.17.1 reads the catalog builds k2_pluspf_20251015, k2_pluspf_20260626 and k2_gtdb_genome_reps_20250609. There are two reasons for one exact release:

  • Kraken2 before 2.17 leaves the domain out. Since 2025, NCBI's taxonomy gives Bacteria, Archaea and Eukaryota the rank "domain", and GTDB's taxonomy uses the same rank. Earlier Kraken2 releases give the report code D only to the older rank name, "superkingdom", so they report these domains as unranked rows (R1, R2), and the OTU table cannot get its domain from them. The table step checks every D and K code against taxo.k2d and stops on such reports (see Troubleshooting).
  • The defaults were measured with 2.17.1. The k-mer evidence settings and the automatic Bracken threshold come from the benchmarks described in Choosing confidence and threshold and Species-level k-mer evidence, run with this release. Kraken2 2.17.2 changes how reads are classified and how minimizers are counted, so those numbers would have to be measured again before moving to it.

docs.title: Downloading
docs.text:
A single wget stream works but is slow on a ~100 GB file. A multi-connection downloader is faster and resumable:

mkdir -p /path/to/db && cd /path/to/db

# k2_pluspf_20260626, one of the builds read by Kraken2 2.17.1 (see Kraken2 version above)
aria2c -x16 -s16 https://genome-idx.s3.amazonaws.com/kraken/k2_pluspf_20260626.tar.gz

# verify integrity against the md5 listed in the catalog
md5sum k2_pluspf_20260626.tar.gz

# contains hash.k2d, opts.k2d, taxo.k2d, *.kmer_distrib
tar -xzf k2_pluspf_20260626.tar.gz

If the AWS CLI is installed, aws s3 cp --no-sign-request <url> is the fastest option (parallel multipart). Plain wget -c <url> also works and resumes a partial download.

Check the free space before extracting

The tarball and the unpacked index sit on disk at the same time, so a full PlusPF build needs room for both.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
This is the part of a shotgun run most likely to go wrong on a shared machine. The whole hash has to be reachable while reads are being classified, and how it gets there is set by one key:

shotgun:
  kraken:
    memory_mapping: true      # true = mmap the DB; false = load it into RAM

Only one of the two strategies applies at runtime.

memory_mapping: true (default) memory_mapping: false How the index is reached the kernel maps the file and pages it in on demand each process reads the whole hash into its own memory Concurrent Kraken2 jobs share the same pages through the operating system's file cache, so parallel jobs do not multiply RAM use each job holds a private full copy Per-process budget MetaFlux requests fixed 20 GB hash.k2d size + 10% Speed comparable to an in-RAM run once the whole hash is cached; I/O-bound for the entire run if it never fits fastest once loaded

Memory mapping is the safer default, and the only workable one when several samples are classified at the same time or when the index is larger than the machine's RAM. Turning it off is worth it when the index comfortably fits in memory and samples are processed one at a time.

The speed row hides two very different cases. Kraken2's lookups land at random across the whole hash, so a memory-mapped run only catches up with an in-RAM one once the entire file sits in the operating system's page cache — that is, when the machine has appreciably more RAM than the index. If the index does not fit, pages are evicted and read back continuously and classification stays I/O-bound from start to finish: hours rather than minutes per sample on a spinning disk or a shared network filesystem. Memory mapping makes an oversized index possible, not fast; where that is the situation, a size-capped build that does fit is the better trade.

How the kraken2 memory request is computed

The memory request for the kraken2 rule is settled at start-up: with memory mapping on it is a flat 20 GB; with it off, the real size of hash.k2d on disk plus 10% headroom, so a 16 GB capped index and a 100 GB PlusPF are handled without editing anything — or, with memory mapping off and hash.k2d not readable yet (the database is still downloading, say), a conservative ~110 GB. This value is what the rule uses, so the resources.mem_mb.kraken2 entry in the config does not override it.

On a cluster this is the value requested from the scheduler, and a job that uses more memory than it requested is killed.

The first Kraken2 call of a run reads the whole database off disk and is slow while the cache is cold; later samples are much faster once the operating system has the pages in memory — provided, as above, that there is room to keep them there.

Threads for the classification step come from resources.threads.kraken2 unless pinned directly:

shotgun:
  kraken:
    threads: null       # null = use resources.threads.kraken2 (16 by default)

docs.title: Bracken settings
docs.text:
Bracken uses the same database directory. Its two settings:

Key Default What it does shotgun.bracken.tax_lev S rank the abundances are re-estimated at — P, C, O, F, G or S; D and K stop the run at start-up shotgun.bracken.threshold auto minimum number of reads Kraken2 must already have put in a taxon's clade for it to enter the re-estimation; auto works it out from each sample's depth, an integer fixes it

tax_lev: S is the usual choice and gives a species-level table. Drop it to G when the index is shallow, or when species-level assignments are not credible for the group in question. The table then has one row per genus.

The threshold is applied to Kraken2's own clade read count for a taxon at the target rank, before Bracken re-estimates anything. Taxa below it are dropped from the model altogether and their reads are discarded rather than redistributed — Bracken prints them in its log as "Total reads discarded".

It is therefore a floor on direct evidence, not on the final estimate, and that has two consequences. A species whose reads Kraken2 mostly parked at genus level — the usual outcome where the database holds several close relatives — can be removed even though redistribution would have credited it with thousands of reads. And because the discarded reads leave the table rather than moving to a surviving relative, the threshold shrinks the total, not just the tail.

A fixed integer is the same number of reads at every depth, so it is a stricter filter, relative to the size of the sample, for a shallow sample than for a deep one. That is why auto, the default, scales the count with depth (see Choosing confidence and threshold). If you set an integer, raise it for deep libraries; lower it if either of the above is a concern, and expect a longer tail of one-read taxa.

The read length Bracken uses is not configurable: it is read per sample from the fastp report and matched to the nearest distribution the database ships (50, 75, 100, 150, 200, 250 or 300 bp). Mixing libraries with very different read lengths in one run is fine — each sample is handled on its own.

docs.title: Host genomes
docs.text: The optional host reference is the other user-supplied database. It is configured under shotgun.decontamination.host_genomes and covered in Decontamination.

docs.title: Decontamination
docs.text:
Two optional steps sit between the raw reads and quality trimming: PhiX removal with BBDuk, and host removal with BBMap. Both exist for the same reason — reads that are not part of the microbial community should not reach the classifier. They cost classification time, they inflate the denominator of every relative abundance, and host reads in particular can be assigned to real microbial taxa when a region of the host genome resembles something in the database.

Both steps are configured in one block:

shotgun:
  decontamination:
    remove_phix: true       # BBDuk vs BBTools' bundled PhiX; false = skip
    host_genomes: []        # list of paths/URLs to FASTA(.gz); [] = skip
    host_min_id: 0.95       # BBMap approximate minimum alignment identity

The chain is raw → (PhiX) → (host) → fastp. Each step reads whatever ran before it, so switching one off is safe: with PhiX removal disabled, host removal reads the raw FASTQs; with both disabled, fastp does. Nothing needs to be renamed and no empty placeholder files are written.

The decontaminated FASTQs are marked temporary — Snakemake deletes them once the next step has consumed them. The statistics files and logs they produce are kept, and are what stats/read_tracking.txt reports on; of the two statistics files, only the BBDuk PhiX one is in a format MultiQC parses.

docs.title: PhiX removal
docs.text:
Rule decontam_phix.

PhiX is the small bacteriophage genome routinely spiked into Illumina runs as a sequencing control. Those reads are genuine sequence and will not be classified as anything real, but removing them early stops them from inflating the denominator of every relative abundance computed downstream.

BBDuk matches reads by k-mer against phix2.fa.gz, BBTools' own copy of the PhiX genome, which ships inside the bbmap conda package: Illumina's phiX174 sequence with two bases corrected and its first 74 bases repeated at the end, so that reads across the point where the circular genome is opened still match. ref=phix loads this file; the package also holds Illumina's own phix174_ill.ref.fa.gz, which ref=phix does not use. Nothing is downloaded and no index is built. The settings are BBTools' own recommendation for PhiX:

bbduk.sh ref=phix in1=... in2=... out1=... out2=... stats=... k=31 hdist=1

k=31 is the match length and hdist=1 allows one mismatch within a k-mer, so a read with a sequencing error still matches.

In raw {sample}_R1/_R2 Out 01.preprocessing/{sample}_dephix_R1/_R2.fastq.gz (temporary), {sample}_dephix_stats.txt Next host removal, or fastp when host removal is off

The stats file carries BBDuk's #Total and #Matched counts, and MultiQC picks it up automatically. The read tracking table takes its raw and nophix columns from the Input: and Result: lines at the end of BBDuk's log, logs/decontam_phix/{sample}.log (halving BBDuk's per-read counts to get read pairs). #Matched would under-count the pairs removed: it counts reads, and BBDuk removes the whole pair when either mate matches PhiX.

Leaving PhiX removal on is the sensible default unless the lab is known to have skipped the spike-in. In shotgun data PhiX is a small fraction anyway, so switching it off costs few reads — but it also removes the only independent count of the reads entering the pipeline, which is what the read-tracking table uses for its raw column.

docs.title: Host removal
docs.text:
Rules fetch_host_refs, build_host_index, decontam_host.

Host removal is alignment-based rather than k-mer-based. BBMap maps the reads against the host reference and MetaFlux keeps the reads that do not map. Alignment is more sensitive than k-mer matching for host reads that differ from the reference assembly — an individual's variants, a related species standing in for the real host — which is the approach the BBTools authors recommend (compare their removehuman.sh).

shotgun:
  decontamination:
    host_genomes:
      - /path/to/human_virus_masked.fasta.gz
      - /path/to/plant_chloroplast.fasta.gz
    host_min_id: 0.95

host_genomes is a YAML list: each reference is its own - item, and each may be a local path or a URL (http, https or ftp). An empty list skips the whole step. Multiple entries are concatenated into a single reference and indexed once, so adding a second host costs one index build, not a second pass over the reads.

Host removal runs through three rules, in this order:

  1. fetch_host_refs resolves every entry — downloading URLs, copying local files, gzipping any plain FASTA — and concatenates them into 01.preprocessing/refs/host_combined.fna.gz. Gzip streams can be joined as they are, so a 3 GB genome is never re-compressed. A local path that does not exist stops the run with a clear error.
  2. build_host_index builds the BBMap index once, under 01.preprocessing/refs/bbmap_index/, and every sample reuses it.
  3. decontam_host maps each sample against that index and writes the unmapped reads (BBMap's outu1/outu2).
In PhiX-filtered reads, or raw reads when PhiX removal is off Out 01.preprocessing/{sample}_dehost_R1/_R2.fastq.gz (temporary), {sample}_dehost_stats.txt Next fastp

BBMap does not print a total/matched table the way BBDuk does, so the rule counts the surviving R1 records itself and writes a single surviving_pairs line. That is what fills the no_host column of stats/read_tracking.txt.

docs.title: Use a masked human reference
docs.text:
For human host removal, the reference should be a masked one. Regions that are conserved across life — ribosomal RNA genes above all — plus low-complexity repeats and stretches with clear homology to bacteria, plants or fungi are masked out of the reference. Without that masking, a bacterial 16S read can align to the human rDNA locus well enough to be removed as host, so microbial reads are lost from the sample.

The masked human reference on Zenodo (Handley 2020, 889 MB) is Brian Bushnell's masked hg19 — ribosomal RNA, plant, animal and fungal homology and low-entropy sequence already taken out, deleted from this file rather than N-filled — with a further layer of viral masking added on top. The first set of masks is what stops real microbial reads being discarded as host. The viral layer additionally keeps human regions homologous to viruses out of the filter: the right behaviour when the viral fraction is of interest, and a small loss of host depletion otherwise.

wget -O /path/to/db/human_virus_masked.fasta.gz \
  "https://zenodo.org/records/4116107/files/human_virus_masked.fasta.gz"

Download it once

A URL in host_genomes is re-fetched by fetch_host_refs on every fresh run. For a ~900 MB reference used repeatedly, download it once and point host_genomes at the local file instead.

The same reasoning applies to non-human hosts. An unmasked plant or insect genome carries the same rRNA and low-complexity traps; if only an unmasked assembly is available, the surviving read counts in stats/read_tracking.txt are worth watching for an implausibly large drop at the no_host column — provided remove_phix: true. With PhiX removal off there is no independent raw count: raw is then read from the fastp report, i.e. from the reads that reached fastp after host removal, so it equals no_host and the drop can never appear. In that case judge the host fraction from BBMap's mapping rate in logs/decontam_host/{sample}.log.

docs.title: host_min_id
docs.text:
host_min_id is BBMap's minid, and the default is 0.95. BBMap's own documentation calls it an approximate minimum alignment identity: it tunes how hard BBMap looks for an alignment rather than imposing a hard cut, so the realised identity of the reads that get removed scatters around the value.

  • Lower (e.g. 0.90) removes more: it catches host reads that diverge from the reference, at the cost of pulling in microbial reads that happen to align reasonably well.
  • Higher (e.g. 0.98) removes less: only near-exact host matches go, so more host survives into the table.

0.95 is a middle setting that suits a reference from the same species as the host. A reference that is only a relative of the true host argues for a lower value.

A methods section that needs a guaranteed cut-off — "host reads were removed at ≥95% identity" — cannot get it from minid. BBMap's idfilter is the explicitly exact parameter for that, and MetaFlux does not set it.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
The host steps are the memory-hungry part of preprocessing. The defaults are sized for a masked human genome, whose BBMap index needs roughly 24–28 GB:

Rule threads mem_mb build_host_index 16 30000 decontam_host 16 30000 decontam_phix 6 4000

All three rules, BBDuk and the two BBMap rules, pass 85% of their mem_mb to the JVM as -Xmx, leaving the rest for the process itself. A smaller host genome can take a smaller budget; a larger one must be given more, or the index build will run out of heap. BBDuk is capped at 6 threads on purpose — it scales poorly beyond four to six threads on a 5 kb reference, so running several samples in parallel is the better use of cores.

docs.title: When BBDuk or BBMap stops on the read pairs
docs.text: BBDuk and BBMap read R1 and R2 in lockstep, one record from each at a time, and require the two files to hold the same number of records in the same order. Read length is not part of that requirement: ragged read lengths, including mates of one pair ending up different lengths, are processed normally.

docs.title: Different numbers of reads in R1 and R2
docs.text:
With the bbmap release MetaFlux pins (39.52), two files that hold different numbers of reads stop decontam_phix with:

java.lang.AssertionError:
There appear to be different numbers of reads in the paired input files.
The pairing may have been corrupted by an upstream process.  It may be fixable by running repair.sh.

The pairing is broken. The usual cause is a library that was filtered before deposition, leaving orphaned mates behind in one file. SRA and BioProject submissions are where this turns up.

Turning PhiX removal off does not get round it. BBMap reads the pair in lockstep too and makes the same requirement, so decontam_host stops on the same input with the same message. With both steps off the run stops at fastp instead, which requires the same thing of the two files:

ERROR: input files don't contain identical amount of reads

Repair the pairing first. repair.sh comes from the same bbmap conda package MetaFlux already installs for decontam_phix and decontam_host, so nothing new has to be added:

repair.sh in1=R1.fastq.gz in2=R2.fastq.gz \
  out1=fixed_R1.fastq.gz out2=fixed_R2.fastq.gz \
  outs=singletons.fastq.gz

It re-syncs the two files on read name and writes the leftover single-ended reads to outs=. Point input.fastq_dir at the repaired files and run again.

Where the raw, untrimmed reads are still available they are the better starting point — they are properly paired, and MetaFlux trims with fastp anyway, so pre-trimmed input buys nothing.

docs.title: List size mismatch
docs.text:
java.lang.AssertionError: List size mismatch: 600 vs 601

This message does not come from the pinned bbmap. It comes from the rewritten BBDuk that bbduk.sh runs in bbmap 39.76 to 40.02: its paired-read reader loses track of mates and stops with this message, or hangs, on correctly paired reads, above all on trimmed reads whose mates differ in length. It prints the same message on broken pairs too, so the message says nothing about the pairing, and repair.sh is no cure.

It means that BBDuk did not come from MetaFlux's environment (workflow/envs/bbtools.yaml, which pins bbmap 39.52). The first lines of logs/decontam_phix/{sample}.log name the version that ran (Version 39.52 for the pinned one). Start the run with --sdm conda, so that Snakemake installs and uses that environment, and keep the pin if you edit the file. MetaFlux before v2.5.0 did not pin bbmap, so its environment could get one of these releases.

docs.title: What to check afterwards
docs.text:
• stats/read_tracking.txt — the nophix and no_host columns, per sample. Both only appear when the step ran. With remove_phix: false the raw column is taken from the fastp report rather than from BBDuk, so it matches no_host exactly.
  • multiqc/multiqc_report.html — the BBDuk PhiX statistics alongside fastp's. BBMap host removal does not appear in MultiQC: {sample}_dehost_stats.txt is a single surviving_pairs count written by MetaFlux, not a format MultiQC parses. BBMap's own mapping rate is in the log below.
  • logs/decontam_host/{sample}.log and logs/build_host_index.log — BBMap's own output, including the mapping rate, if a sample looks wrong.

docs.title: Species-level k-mer evidence
docs.text:
Read this after Choosing confidence and threshold

Bracken's depth-scaled read threshold, described on that page, has the largest effect on precision in shotgun mode; set it first. This gate catches one narrow kind of error that the threshold cannot detect. It is off by default; see Why the default is enabled: false.

Kraken2's read count tells you how many reads it chose to label with a taxon. It does not tell you how much sequence unique to that organism actually turned up in the sample — and those are different questions.

  • A species that is genuinely present contributes many different species-specific sequences.
  • A spurious call is usually a small set of sequences — conserved, repetitive, or shared with a relative that really is abundant — matched over and over.

In a read count the two look identical. Running Kraken2 with --report-minimizer-data adds the number that separates them. MetaFlux always does.

docs.title: The two extra columns
docs.text:
The report becomes eight columns instead of six, with two inserted before the rank code:

Column Contents 4 Number of minimizers in the read data associated with this taxon 5 An estimate of the number of distinct minimizers in the read data associated with this taxon

Column 5 is an estimate, not an exact count — Kraken2 uses a HyperLogLog sketch rather than storing every minimizer. Both columns are clade-cumulative, like the read counts.

What "associated with this taxon" actually means

The columns do not count the minimizers carried by the reads assigned to the taxon.

Kraken2 attributes each minimizer occurrence to whichever taxon that minimizer maps to in the database (its lowest common ancestor), pooled over every read in the sample, regardless of where each read finally got assigned.

This is visible in any report: taxa with two or three assigned reads can carry hundreds of thousands of minimizer counts. In SRR39106521, one of the test samples described below, the genus row Streptomyces has 3 clade reads and 343,359 total minimizers, about 500 times the 690 k-mer positions that three pairs of 149-base reads can hold. Counts that high cannot come from the assigned reads alone; they are expected when minimizers are attributed by LCA.

So column 5 for a species means: how many distinct database minimizers specific to that species were seen anywhere in this sample. That is a statement about how much species-specific sequence is present — the minimizer counterpart of what KrakenUniq calls unique k-mers, so the published thresholds below are a fair starting point; how well they convert to minimizers is discussed below. It is not a genome-coverage measure, and describing it as "how much of the genome the reads covered" would be wrong.

The flag itself changes no classification

--report-minimizer-data is purely additive reporting: with or without it, Kraken2 writes a byte-for-byte identical per-read output and the same values in every shared report column.

docs.title: Reading the numbers
docs.text:
Two species from SRR39106521, with similar read counts:

Species Reads Distinct minimizers Total minimizers Duplicity Pseudomonas aeruginosa 4,775 68,276 221,570 3.2 Pigmentiphaga sp. CHJ604 4,129 929 226,726 244.1

The two also have almost the same total minimizer count. The first is supported by 68,276 distinct species-specific minimizers. The second is supported by 929, each one seen about 240 times.

Duplicity (total ÷ distinct) is the most directly readable of the three numbers, because it does not require knowing the sequencing depth. It also barely tracks abundance: across the 2,418 species rows in the Kraken2 reports of the four test samples, Pearson r against log reads is +0.17 for log duplicity and +0.71 for the log distinct count. That makes it the better number to eyeball. It is nonetheless a worse filter (see What does not work), so MetaFlux reports it and thresholds the distinct count.

docs.title: What MetaFlux writes
docs.text:
Every shotgun run produces these, per sample, whether or not the gate is switched on:

02.classification/kraken2/{sample}_species_evidence.tsv   one row per taxon at the Bracken rank
02.classification/kraken2/{sample}_report_gated.txt       the report with failing taxa removed
stats/kmer_evidence/{sample}_evidence.png                 reads vs distinct minimizers, log-log

The gated report is written even when the gate is off, precisely so you can diff it against the Kraken2 report and see what enabling the gate would do to your data before trusting it.

The evidence table carries, per taxon: taxid, name, rank, clade and direct reads, total and distinct minimizers, duplicity, minimizers per read, percent of classified reads, and the verdict with its reason.

docs.title: The gate
docs.text:
shotgun:
  kmer_evidence:
    enabled: false                     # report only; pipeline unchanged
    min_distinct_minimizers: 300       # the floor; see the unit conversion below
    min_reads: 0                       # extra read floor, applied together with the above
    never_prune_above_fraction: 0.01   # safety rail

docs.title: Where it acts
docs.text:
kraken2  →  kmer_evidence  →  bracken  →  finalize_otu_table

The gate sits between Kraken2 and Bracken. It does not replace or skip Bracken — it hands Bracken a cleaned report instead of the raw one. Because the correction happens upstream, it flows all the way through: otu_table.biom and otu_table.tsv become the corrected tables. There is no separate filtered file to reconcile.

Switching the gate off restores the previous behaviour exactly: Bracken reads Kraken2's own report and nothing downstream changes.

docs.title: How a taxon is removed
docs.text:
Two details must be handled correctly; otherwise Bracken redistributes the reads of the pruned report wrongly, without an error.

Whole subtree, never a bare row. Bracken rebuilds the taxonomy tree from the indentation of the report, attaching each row to the last row one level above it. Delete a species row and leave its strain (S1) children behind, and those children get re-parented onto whichever species happens to precede them, whose read count is then inflated without any warning. So when a taxon fails, everything indented beneath it goes too.

The reads are credited to the parent, not discarded. A pruned taxon's whole clade total is added to its parent's own-node count, so Bracken redistributes those reads among the siblings that passed. The parent's clade total is untouched, so the report's arithmetic still balances: for every node, clade == direct + sum(children clade), and no column other than a parent's direct count ever changes.

Two things this does not guarantee

Not all reads land on close relatives. The rationale for crediting the parent is that a spurious call usually borrows evidence from a neighbour. That holds for most of the reads that move, not all: part of them cross genus or family boundaries.

Some reads are still lost. If every species under a genus fails, Bracken has nothing left at the target rank to redistribute to, and drops those reads, usually a small fraction of the sample. Crediting the parent is much better than deleting rows outright, but it is not conservation.

docs.title: Choosing a threshold
docs.text:
Three published sources give thresholds for this kind of filter, all expressed in KrakenUniq's unique k-mers:

Source What it reports KrakenUniq (Breitwieser, Baker & Salzberg, 2018) On a synthetic mix of reads from bacterial isolates (1–34 million read pairs), the best threshold (highest recall at a false discovery rate of 5 % or less) rose by about 2,000 unique k-mers per million reads sequenced: about 3,700 at 1 million, 21,000 at 10 million. For ten patient biopsies, mostly host DNA, a fixed 1,000 unique k-mers together with at least 10 reads removed the background calls and kept every confirmed pathogen. Oskolkov (2026), Front. Microbiol. 17:1603339 Simulated ancient metagenomes (fragments of about 42 bases, 0.1–0.7 million reads): about 1,000 unique k-mers gave the best F1, and a read-count filter added nothing. The best value rose with depth, by about 200 unique k-mers per 100,000 reads, a trend the paper calls relatively weak. Run on the same data, Kraken2 needed two to three times more distinct minimizers than KrakenUniq needed unique k-mers. aMeta (Pochon et al., 2023) Defaults of 1,000 unique k-mers and 200 assigned reads, set from more than 1,200 ancient libraries; users are invited to try 500–1,500 k-mers depending on depth. The 2026 study above comes from the same group and reuses aMeta's simulated data.

Published thresholds count k-mers; Kraken2 reports minimizers

In plain terms. Kraken2 reads a sequence as overlapping 35-base k-mers, but it does not look each one up. For every k-mer it picks one 31-base piece inside it, the minimizer, and stores and counts only that. Neighbouring k-mers usually pick the same piece, so a region of a genome gives about three times fewer distinct minimizers than distinct k-mers. The studies above counted unique k-mers and settled on about 1,000. In a Kraken2 report the same amount of sequence shows up as about 333 distinct minimizers.
