The default floor, 300, is that figure rounded down, because the conversion is only approximate. It was not tuned on MetaFlux's own test data, and it is a low, cautious value rather than an exact equivalent. When Oskolkov (2026) ran both tools on the same simulated data, the best Kraken2 floor was two to three times higher than the best KrakenUniq one, where the conversion predicts three times lower, and MetaFlux's own benchmark finds useful floors in the thousands (see Scaling the floor with depth).

The arithmetic, for a database built with other settings. How many k-mers share a minimizer depends on the database's k and l. Each k-mer of length k spans w = k − l + 1 candidate minimizer positions of length l, and the standard expected density of selected minimizers is 2 / (w + 1). For the usual nucleotide settings (k = 35, l = 31) that is w = 5 and a density of 1/3 — roughly one distinct minimizer per three k-mers.

So, counting sequence alone, a published 1,000 unique k-mers corresponds to about 333 distinct minimizers here.

Check k and l on the first line of your database's inspect.txt and recompute if they differ. (The 2/(w+1) density is the expectation for a random minimizer scheme; Kraken2's spaced-seed masking shifts it slightly, so treat 333 as an approximate conversion, not an exact one.)

docs.title: What it does on real data
docs.text:
The numbers below come from the four metagenomes of BioProject PRJNA1477390 (runs SRR39106521–SRR39106524), microbial consortia enriched on naproxen from wastewater treatment plants (see Shotgun test dataset). They were processed with the MetaFlux v2.5.0 defaults (Kraken2 confidence 0.15, Bracken threshold: auto) and PlusPF k2_pluspf_20260626, once with the gate off and once with it on at the default floor of 300. The floor is min_distinct_minimizers: the number of distinct minimizers a species needs in the Kraken2 report to stay in the table.

SRR39106521 SRR39106522 SRR39106523 SRR39106524 Species in otu_table.tsv, gate off 99 80 116 120 Species, gate on (floor 300) 84 66 94 104 Genera, gate off → on 39 → 34 31 → 28 46 → 39 52 → 44 Read pairs moved to another species 4.9 % 1.3 % 5.8 % 1.8 % Change in total read pairs −0.01 % +0.01 % −0.01 % −0.09 % Genomes detected by sylph in the same reads 10 9 14 16 Species above 1 % of otu_table.tsv, gate off 21 10 23 12 Abundant members counted from the 16S rRNA gene, no reference 7 6 4 10
  • The gate removes 14 to 22 species per sample and almost no reads. The reads of a removed species go back to its parent taxon, and Bracken shares them among the relatives that passed.
  • The removed species are not only rare ones. Bracken spreads the reads that Kraken2 could only place at genus level or above over the species below, and it had given the removed species 10 to 27 times more reads than Kraken2 assigned to them. In every sample one of the 20 most abundant species is removed. The largest case is Pseudomonas sp. JS425 in SRR39106521: 372 read pairs from Kraken2, carrying 182 distinct minimizers, raised by Bracken to 69,992 read pairs, the eighth most abundant species in the sample. Its read count passes the Bracken threshold; only the distinct-minimizer count shows how little species-specific sequence is behind it (more below).
  • Fewer species is the right direction for these samples. sylph, run by MetaFlux in both mode against gtdb-r232-c200-dbv1 and fungi-refseq-2025-10-11-c200-dbv1, detects 9 to 16 genomes per sample; it misses organisms without a closely related reference genome. A count that needs no reference database comes from the 16S rRNA gene fragments in the reads, extracted with Metaxa2 2.2.3: fragments from the same part of the gene are compared with one another and grouped at 97 % identity. It sees only the more abundant members, roughly those above 1–2 % of the 16S gene copies, and finds 4 to 10 per sample, mostly from the same families that sylph and Kraken2 report. For that abundant part of the community Kraken2 reports 10 to 23 species, those above 1 % of its table, because it splits the reads of one organism over several related species.
  • The gate does not bring the list down to that size. Most of what remains is a database problem. The most abundant organism in SRR39106521 and SRR39106523, Pusillimonas noertemannii, has no genome in PlusPF. Its reads are reported under several Achromobacter species, which together hold more than half of each of these two tables; the largest of them have tens of thousands of distinct minimizers (see the warning on missing organisms in Databases). A k-mer floor cannot correct that.

The same four samples at other floors: species left in otu_table.tsv, and the share of the gate-off table held by the species that the floor removes.

Floor SRR39106521 SRR39106522 SRR39106523 SRR39106524 Read pairs held by removed species none (gate off) 99 80 116 120 0 200 92 73 105 112 0.9–4.7 % 300 (default) 84 66 94 104 1.3–5.8 % 1,000 55 44 61 80 8–21 % 3,000 29 26 31 54 13–42 %

A lower floor keeps the species with 200 to 300 distinct minimizers, 7 to 11 more per sample. These samples have no known composition, so they cannot show whether those species are real. A higher floor removes many more species but also moves a large share of the table: at 3,000, 13 to 42 % of the read pairs end up under a different species. On benchmark communities of known composition, a fixed floor of 10,000 already lowered some samples' F1 by removing true species, and lower fixed floors did the same once shallower sequencing was modelled (3,000 at 30 % of the depth, 1,000 at 10 %). A floor scaled to the depth of the sample avoids this; see the next section.

docs.title: Scaling the floor with depth
docs.text:
A species that is really present leaves more distinct minimizers the deeper a sample is sequenced, and so, up to a limit, does a spurious call that borrows sequence from an abundant relative. A fixed floor is therefore lenient on deep samples and strict on shallow ones. KrakenUniq and Oskolkov (2026) reported the same for unique k-mers (table above), but neither gives a depth rule for Kraken2.

MetaFlux's benchmark was used to fit one. It covers 42 samples of known composition: one real mock community (ZymoBIOMICS D6331, SRA run SRR38976715, BioProject PRJNA1474435) and 41 simulated CAMI II samples from the marine, rhizosphere and strain-madness sets (see Benchmark data), with 2.6–6.5 million classified read pairs each, classified with three Kraken2 indices: k2_pluspf_20260626 (at confidence 0.15 and 0.20), k2_gtdb_genome_reps_20250609 (GTDB r226 representative genomes) and k2_NCBI_reference_20251007 (one genome per NCBI species). A floor of one distinct minimizer per 1,000 classified read pairs gave the best result that was safe everywhere:

  • species-level F1 rose by 0.066 on average (0.036 with PlusPF), against 0.0020 for the fixed default of 300 (0.0003 with PlusPF);
  • it removed 2,288 of 13,115 false species calls and 6 of 13,419 true ones (none with PlusPF), and lowered no sample's F1;
  • it stayed safe when shallower sequencing was modelled, down to 1 % of the reads, while every fixed floor tested, from 300 to 10,000, lowered some samples' F1 at some depth.

This is the same order of magnitude as KrakenUniq's slope (about 670 distinct minimizers per million read pairs once converted), but the number itself comes from MetaFlux's benchmark. As a starting point:

Classified read pairs in the shallowest sample, host excluded min_distinct_minimizers 500,000 500 1 million 1,000 2 million 2,000 5 million 5,000 6.5 million or more 6,500

Each sample's classified count is in stats/read_tracking.txt (column classified) and in its Bracken log ([bracken] auto threshold: 5e-05 x N classified read pairs). MetaFlux applies one floor to every sample in a run, so size it on the shallowest sample; the deeper samples then get a more lenient floor than they could take. Below about 500,000 classified pairs the scaled floor gains little. Use it even when it comes out lower than the default of 300: in benchmark samples thinned to 26,000–195,000 classified pairs, the fixed floor of 300 lowered some samples' F1 and the scaled floor lowered none.

Limits of this rule:

  • It rests on limited data. Three quarters of the F1 gain came from the one real mock community; on the simulated CAMI samples it was 0.01–0.03. The shallower depths were modelled from the observed counts, not sequenced.
  • Do not go above 1.5 per 1,000 pairs. At that rate rare true species start to be removed (92 of 13,419 true calls), and from 2 per 1,000 some samples' F1 falls even at full depth.
  • Do not go above 6,500 for deeper samples. The benchmark stops at 6.5 million classified pairs. A floor that keeps growing with depth eventually exceeds what a real species with a small species-specific part of its genome can reach; in the model this began at about 10 million pairs.
  • Exclude host reads. PlusPF contains the human genome and host removal is off by default, so host reads would raise the floor without adding any microbial evidence. Subtract the read pairs Kraken2 assigned to the host (for human, the Homo sapiens row of the report), or remove the host first (Decontamination).
  • Library layout. The rule assumes paired 2×150 bp Illumina reads with little mate overlap and few duplicates. Shorter reads, single-end data, overlapping mates and duplicate-rich libraries give fewer distinct minimizers per read pair, so the same floor is stricter for them; use a lower value.
  • It changes the table more than 300 does. On the test dataset above (1.7–3.5 million classified pairs), a floor of 1,673, sized on the shallowest sample with its host reads excluded, keeps 33–68 species per sample, against 66–104 at 300, and the species it removes hold 10–33 % of the read pairs, which move to relatives. That is still well above the 9–16 genomes sylph finds. Compare otu_table.tsv with the gate off and on before relying on it.

docs.title: Why the default is enabled: false
docs.text:
The gate is off by default because a correctly scaled Bracken threshold already removes most of what it would remove. It has been run on 46 samples: the D6331 mock, the four PRJNA1477390 metagenomes and 41 CAMI II samples. In gate-on/gate-off runs of CAMI II samples at several depths with PlusPF k2_pluspf_20251015, the gate changed species-level F1 by a mean of +0.0009 at the depth-scaled threshold, and by zero on the strain-madness and rhizosphere samples at every depth tested. At the former fixed -t 10 the mean was +0.0079, about nine times more. So the gate mainly helps when the Bracken threshold is not scaled to depth; with a scaled threshold it adds little.

Which database build those two numbers come from

Both figures come from gate-on/gate-off runs on PlusPF k2_pluspf_20251015 (15 sample-depth combinations at the scaled threshold, 11 at the fixed one). The k2_pluspf_20260626 benchmark runs had the gate off; removing from their Bracken output the species the gate would prune at the default floor of 300 changes mean species-level F1 by +0.0003.

docs.title: Unchanged F1 does not mean an unchanged table
docs.text:
The two filters ask different questions. The threshold asks how many reads; the gate asks how much distinct sequence. A taxon can pass one and fail the other, and an aggregate score of 250+ species barely notices when a single one flips.

Pseudomonas sp. JS425 in the four test samples, with the Bracken threshold scaled to depth (threshold_alpha 5×10⁻⁵):

Sample Classified pairs Bracken -t Kraken2 pairs Distinct minimizers Passes -t After Bracken, gate off Gate SRR39106521 2,268,774 113 372 182 yes 69,992 removed SRR39106522 3,458,847 173 103 181 no – removed SRR39106523 1,673,810 84 301 181 yes 51,418 removed SRR39106524 2,177,429 109 123 181 yes 8,935 removed

In SRR39106521 the 372 read pairs pass the threshold, but they rest on 182 distinct minimizers, each hit about 60 times, and Bracken raises the call to 3 % of the sample. The threshold keeps JS425 in three samples and drops it from the fourth only because the cut-off falls differently there; in a presence/absence plot that would look like a real difference between samples. The gate removes it from all four.

These samples have no known composition, so they do not enter the F1 scores above. That is why the benchmark shows almost no gain from the gate while the table changes.

When to consider turning it on: communities the database covers poorly, where reads from organisms absent from the database are assigned to their relatives. The evidence for this is limited. It rests on cases like JS425 in the wastewater test samples, which have no known composition; on the CAMI II rhizosphere samples, the poorly covered benchmark set with a known composition, the gate hardly changed F1. For gut, clinical or other samples close to RefSeq, leave it off. Either way the gated report is written even when the gate is off, so compare it with the Kraken2 report before deciding.

docs.title: Validation status
docs.text: What the gate was tested against, and what those tests could and could not show.

docs.title: What has been checked
docs.text:
The gate was checked on one real mock community (Zymo D6331, below) and on CAMI II's marine, rhizosphere and strain-madness gold-standard sets (41 samples): in gate-on/gate-off runs with PlusPF k2_pluspf_20251015, and by applying it to the Bracken calls of the k2_pluspf_20260626 runs. These results were scored with the benchmark's own scorer. On the two k2_pluspf_20260626 runs (Kraken2 confidence 0.15 and 0.20) that scorer was checked against OPAL 1.0.13, the CAMI assessment tool: given the same input preparation, OPAL's species-level counts of true positives, false positives and false negatives equal the scorer's in every sample. The full methodology and the numbers that matter for choosing a threshold are on the confidence and threshold page. The result for this gate: once the Bracken threshold is scaled to depth it adds at most 0.002 F1 (PlusPF k2_pluspf_20251015), but it still removes calls like JS425 above, which a read-count threshold cannot detect.

One real mock community: the ZymoBIOMICS Gut Microbiome Standard (D6331), SRA run SRR38976715 (BioProject PRJNA1474435; see Benchmark data), with about 5.3 million classified read pairs.

The standard is sold as 21 strains. A species-level profiler can only ever see 17 species, because five of the 21 are Escherichia coli strains at 2.8% each that collapse into one E. coli row at 14%. That ceiling is arithmetic, not a reference-database gap. Zymo lists the standard's Fusobacterium as F. nucleatum (strain 2/1/50A), but sylph (GTDB r232), MetaPhlAn 4 and Kraken2 with GTDB r226 or PlusPF k2_pluspf_20260626 place most of these reads in F. animalis, a former subspecies of F. nucleatum now ranked as a species. It is therefore scored as F. animalis, and calls of F. nucleatum, F. polymorphum and F. vincentii count as false positives. Homo sapiens, from human DNA in the sample, is not scored.

The run was processed twice through the pipeline with PlusPF k2_pluspf_20251015, Kraken2 confidence 0.15 and Bracken at the former fixed -t 10: once with the gate off and once with it on at a floor of 333. A floor of 300 gives the same species list on this run. At the current default threshold (-t 265 for this run), only 2 of the 34 false positives in the table below have enough reads to pass (F. nucleatum and F. polymorphum), as does the unscored Homo sapiens; the gate removes none of them, and the threshold itself drops Salmonella enterica.

Gate off Gate on True members recovered 15 / 17 15 / 17 False-positive species 34 22 Precision 0.306 0.405 F1 0.455 0.556
  • No true member was removed. Salmonella enterica, 0.01% of the standard and 134 classified reads, has 3,547 distinct minimizers at a duplicity of 1.5, more than ten times the floor, and is kept. The gate depends on this difference: a rare species can still have many distinct minimizers.
  • The two members never recovered (Enterococcus faecalis at 0.001%, Clostridium perfringens at 0.0001%) have one Kraken2 read each, below Bracken's -t 10, so neither reaches the table in either run. Both have species entries in the database, so they were missed for lack of reads.
  • Quantitative accuracy did not change. With the human row left out, L1 distance to the theoretical composition was 47.15 without the gate and 47.14 with it, Shannon H 2.145 and 2.144, and the Bray–Curtis dissimilarity between the two profiles 0.00009. The 82 taxa the gate removed at 333 held 426 of the 5.3 million reads (81 taxa and 423 reads at 300). Any ordination or differential-abundance test would give the same answer from both tables.
  • Richness, on the other hand, improved substantially — which is where the gate did its work on this dataset:
Observed richness Truth Gate off Gate on Species 17 49 (+188%) 37 (+118%) Genera 17 25 (+47%) 18 (+6%)

On this mock the gate changed which species are listed, not their abundances. If you report how many taxa you detected, or work with presence/absence, that matters. If you only ever compare relative abundances between samples, on data like this it will not change your conclusions.

docs.title: Why richness is still over-estimated with the gate on
docs.text:
With the gate on, 37 species other than human are still reported against 17 in the standard. Most of the 22 false positives are not the kind of call the gate is designed to remove.

Of the 22 false-positive species that survive, 19 are congeners of a genuine member — and the other three are defensible. The table also lists Homo sapiens, which is not scored:

Survivor Reads after Bracken Distinct minimizers What it is Fusobacterium nucleatum, F. vincentii, F. polymorphum 180,835 947–29,678 Close relatives of the true member, F. animalis; all four were subspecies of F. nucleatum until F. animalis, F. vincentii and F. polymorphum were raised to species rank. With k2_pluspf_20251015, Kraken2 gives F. nucleatum more reads than F. animalis (16,709 against 6,062) Homo sapiens 965 10,062 Trace human DNA from handling; present in the sample, a contaminant that is not scored Shigella dysenteriae 839 1,117 Shigella sits phylogenetically inside E. coli; the genomes are near-identical Sphingomonas paucimobilis, Cutibacterium acnes 51 464–779 Common extraction-kit and skin contaminants; plausibly present in the sample 16 further congeners of Veillonella, Fusobacterium, Saccharomyces, Escherichia, Bacteroides, Candida, Clostridioides 1,874 400–5,380 Close relatives of an abundant true member

All these survivors carry large distinct-minimizer counts — Saccharomyces paradoxus has 5,380 on just 73 reads, at a duplicity of 1.7. That is broad, un-repetitive evidence, and it is genuinely in the read data: S. cerevisiae is a real member of the standard, and its sequence matches a great deal of what the database files under its sister species.

So there are two different ways a species-level call goes wrong, and only one is an evidence problem:

  • Thin evidence — a few conserved minimizers hit over and over. Low distinct count, high duplicity. The gate removes these.
  • Mis-attributed evidence — a genuinely present organism whose sequence matches a close relative's database entry. High distinct count, low duplicity. The gate does not remove these, and should not: the sequence is in the sample, and only the species label is wrong.

The residual inflation is almost entirely the second kind, which is a property of how finely the reference database splits closely related organisms — not something any k-mer counting method can detect. The practical consequence is visible in the table above: at genus rank, where those distinctions disappear, the gate brings richness from +47% to +6% of the true value.

docs.title: What this does not show
docs.text:
On the mock the gate removed no true species; on CAMI II it changed F1 very little

Every organism in D6331 has a species-level entry in the database used. When that is true, classification is already close to correct, most false positives are a thin tail of taxa with few reads, and there is little for an evidence filter to repair, which is what the CAMI II benchmark found: with the Bracken threshold scaled to depth, this gate adds at most 0.002 F1 across marine, rhizosphere and strain-madness samples (PlusPF k2_pluspf_20251015).

The gate is still useful in cases like JS425 above: a taxon with an ordinary read count but few distinct minimizers. A read-count threshold cannot detect this, however it is scaled.

The CAMI II benchmark described on the confidence and threshold page covers what one mock cannot: larger and more even communities (marine, 256–381 species per sample), several samples at several depths, communities with genomes absent from the reference (rhizosphere: only 165 of its 307 gold-standard species, 54 %, are in PlusPF k2_pluspf_20260626), and sample types beyond gut and wastewater. It agrees with the D6331 result that the gate removes no true species at full sequencing depth, and it shows that once the Bracken threshold is scaled to depth the gate changes F1 very little.

Still untested: everything above used short-read Illumina data. Long-read or hybrid data, and sample types with sparser reference coverage than rhizosphere, have not been tried. If you switch the gate on, check the evidence tables for what it removed.

docs.title: Limitation: very close relatives
docs.text: Very close relatives defeat the method, and no k-mer evidence measure fixes this. Shigella dysenteriae is not in D6331, but 13 reads were assigned to it — carrying 1,117 distinct minimizers, so it passes the gate, and Bracken raised it to 839 reads (834 with the gate off). Shigella and E. coli are similar enough that minimizers the database marks as Shigella-specific are genuinely present in E. coli reads. That is a property of the reference taxonomy, not something this filter can detect.

docs.title: Threshold stability
docs.text:
A fixed threshold should give a species the same verdict in every sample, but it does not always. Of 620 species found in more than one of the four PRJNA1477390 test samples, 123 (20 %) got different verdicts at the floor of 300:

  • 62 % differ mainly in depth: the species had at least five times fewer reads in one sample, and with few reads it cannot reach enough distinct minimizers. This change of verdict is probably correct.
  • 38 % have read counts less than five-fold apart. 20 of these 47 species lie close to the floor, between 200 and 450 distinct minimizers, in every sample. Sphingomonas paucimobilis is one: 155 to 199 read pairs in each sample, 350 distinct minimizers in SRR39106524 (kept) and 277 to 295 in the other three (removed). The other 27 lie further from the floor in at least one sample, sometimes much further: Sphingopyxis lindanitolerans has 93 to 105 distinct minimizers in three samples and 10,626 in the fourth, on 95 to 282 read pairs.

Any fixed cut-off behaves like this, whatever its value. Check the evidence tables for species whose verdict differs between samples.

docs.title: What does not work
docs.text:
Three approaches were tested on the four PRJNA1477390 test samples and rejected. They are described here because each seems reasonable before it is measured.

A threshold on distinct minimizers alone is partly an abundance filter. The distinct count correlates with read count (Pearson r = +0.71 on log-log across the 2,418 species rows of the four Kraken2 reports), so some of what it removes, it removes for being rare. This is why the published thresholds pair the k-mer count with an explicit read floor — min_reads exists for exactly that, and is 0 by default only because Oskolkov (2026) found that filtering on unique k-mers alone was enough to reach the best F1, with no read-count filter needed.

Normalising to minimizers-per-read inverts the filter. That ratio falls as abundance rises (r = −0.72): across the four samples its median is 84 for single-read species and 1.4 for species with 1,000 reads or more. A "ratio below 5" rule on SRR39106521 removed 80 % of the reads that had reached species rank, including the two species with the most reads, while keeping all 160 single-read species.

Thresholding duplicity removes the most abundant species. Across all species rows duplicity hardly changes with abundance (r = +0.17), but the most deeply sequenced species have high values, because each of their minimizers is seen many times. Achromobacter denitrificans, the largest species in all four samples, has a duplicity of 23 to 74 on 42,000 to 1.1 million distinct minimizers. A duplicity cut-off of 10 prunes about as many species rows as the floor of 300 (65 % against 66 %), and its verdicts differ between samples less often (14 % of species against 20 %). But it would remove 73 to 93 % of each sample's table, A. denitrificans included, where the floor of 300 removes 1.3 to 5.8 %. With the gate's 1 % safety rail, which would keep A. denitrificans, it would still remove 16 to 65 %. Duplicity is therefore reported, not thresholded.

Flagging outliers against a fitted trend line finds no distinct population. Fitting log(distinct minimizers) against log(reads) and taking residuals looks principled, but the residuals are essentially normal: in SRR39106521 a "2 SD below the line" rule flagged 14 of 578 species, where a normal distribution predicts 13.1. There is no separable cluster to find, so the rule just removes the bottom few percent of any sample. Worse, because the line is fitted per sample, the same species can fall on opposite sides of it in different samples of one study.

The conclusion for the design: use one fixed floor for every sample of a run, so that every sample is judged against the same number, and treat the trend line as a ranking for the eye rather than a test.

docs.title: Shotgun mode overview
docs.text:
Shotgun mode profiles whole-metagenome Illumina libraries. There is no PCR and no primer: every read pair that comes off the sequencer is matched against a k-mer database, so what limits the result is sequencing depth and the reference database rather than the resolving power of one marker gene.

Is shotgun mode the right tool for your samples?

This path targets environmental communities. For host-associated or food samples a marker-gene profiler is usually more precise — see what shotgun mode is for.

The pipeline is Kraken2 for read classification and Bracken for abundance re-estimation, with decontamination and quality trimming in front of them and a combined OTU table at the end. It is selected with one config key:

mode: shotgun          # amplicon | shotgun

The mode can also be set on the command line without editing the file: --config mode=shotgun. Which mode suits which data is covered in Choosing a mode.

mode must match the data

Both modes accept {sample}_R1 / {sample}_R2 filenames, so pointing a shotgun run at amplicon data (or the reverse) does not always produce an error; the run can finish with the wrong analysis. Check mode before every run.

Shotgun mode needs reference data that MetaFlux does not fetch: a Kraken2 database for the default profiler, sylph databases and their lineage tables for profiler: sylph, and both for profiler: both. See Reference databases.

docs.title: The chain
docs.text:
raw R1/R2 ──▶ BBDuk PhiX* ──▶ BBMap host* ──▶ fastp ──▶ Kraken2 ──▶ Bracken ──▶ OTU table
                _dephix         _dehost        _trim      report      report     .tsv + .biom
                                                            │
                                                            └──▶ KrakenTools per-taxon reads*

  * optional, toggled in config

sylph instead of Kraken2, or next to it

With shotgun.profiler: sylph, sylph replaces everything from Kraken2 onwards: it estimates genome abundances from k-mer sketches of the same trimmed reads and writes 03.abundance/sylph_table.tsv. With both, the two chains run side by side on the same reads and their tables are never merged. The cleaning steps are the same in every case. See sylph.

Each stage writes files tagged with the step it came off (_dephix, _dehost, _trim). When an optional step is switched off, the next step reads the output of the last step that ran, and no placeholder files are written.

The rules carry descending Snakemake priorities (download_sra 10 down to finalize_otu_table 1), so when many jobs are ready at once the scheduler works through the early stages first rather than starting classification while reads are still being fetched.

docs.title: 1. Input — local FASTQs or a BioProject
docs.text:
Reads come from one of two places.

Local files in input.fastq_dir. Shotgun mode accepts either naming convention and detects which one is in use:

Layout Example Where it usually comes from {sample}_R1 / {sample}_R2 soil01_R1.fastq.gz Illumina/bcl2fastq output, MetaFlux's default {sample}_1 / {sample}_2 SRR11605259_1.fastq.gz raw fasterq-dump output

Reads must carry the fastq.gz extension, or plain fastq if uncompressed. fq and fq.gz are accepted by the start-up check but are never resolved afterwards — the rules look only for .fastq.gz and .fastq — and in shotgun mode the missing .fastq.gz path matches the download_sra rule under _R1/_R2 naming, so the run tries to fetch each local sample from SRA rather than reporting that the extension is unsupported; with _1/_2 naming it stops with a missing-input error instead. The check itself sees only the R1 files: a mixture of extensions among them stops the run at start-up, but the R2 files are never inspected, so uniformity across the directory is not enforced.

Direct from NCBI SRA. Setting input.bioproject to a BioProject accession makes MetaFlux resolve that project's runs itself:

input:
  fastq_dir: /path/to/fastq_dir      # must be writable — downloads land here
  bioproject: PRJNA603575
  accession_list: null               # e.g. [SRR11605259, SRR11605260]

The accession is resolved through NCBI e-utils (esearch then efetch for the runinfo table) and the run list is cached in fastq_dir as {BIOPROJECT}_runinfo.csv, so a re-run does not query NCBI again. Only runs whose LibraryLayout is PAIRED are kept — single-end runs do not fit the rest of the pipeline. accession_list narrows that set further, which is how a project that mixes WGS with amplicon or RNA-Seq runs is reduced to the metagenomes.

Each run is then fetched with prefetch and unpacked with fasterq-dump (--split-files --skip-technical), and the two mates are compressed to {sample}_R1.fastq.gz / {sample}_R2.fastq.gz in fastq_dir — so downstream rules see the same filenames whether the data was downloaded or already local.

Whatever the source, the sample list is written to samples.tsv at the top of the output directory, with one row per sample: sample, source (local or bioproject), bioproject, r1, r2. It exists so downstream R or Python scripts can read the manifest instead of re-parsing the config or globbing the FASTQ directory again.

docs.title: 2. PhiX removal (optional)
docs.text:
Rule decontam_phix — off with shotgun.decontamination.remove_phix: false.

PhiX is the control genome spiked into most Illumina runs; those reads are real sequence but they are not part of the sample. BBDuk matches the reads against the PhiX reference bundled inside the BBTools package, so nothing is downloaded or indexed.

Input: the raw FASTQs. Output: {sample}_dephix_R1/_R2.fastq.gz (temporary — see below) plus {sample}_dephix_stats.txt, which feeds MultiQC; the read tracking table takes its PhiX counts from BBDuk's log. Consumed by the host step, or by fastp when host removal is off.

BBDuk needs R1 and R2 to be properly paired

BBDuk reads the two files in lockstep and requires them to hold the same number of records in the same order. Read length does not matter — ragged reads, and mates of a pair with different lengths, are processed normally. A crash with There appear to be different numbers of reads in the paired input files means the pairing is broken, usually because reads were filtered before deposition and orphaned mates were left in one file — common for SRA data. repair.sh, from the same BBTools package, puts the files back in step. A crash with AssertionError: List size mismatch: N vs M is different: it comes from newer bbmap releases (39.76 to 40.02), which print it on correctly paired reads too, and the cure is MetaFlux's pinned environment, not repair.sh. Details are in Decontamination.

docs.title: 3. Host and contaminant removal (optional)
docs.text:
Rules fetch_host_refs, build_host_index, decontam_host — off when shotgun.decontamination.host_genomes is an empty list.

Host DNA dominates many metagenomes (gut, skin, plant tissue) and, left in, it costs classification time and can be mis-assigned to microbial taxa. BBMap aligns the reads against one or more user-supplied genomes and keeps only the reads that do not map.

Input: the PhiX-filtered reads, or the raw reads when PhiX removal is off. Output: {sample}_dehost_R1/_R2.fastq.gz plus {sample}_dehost_stats.txt with the surviving pair count. Consumed by fastp.

Which reference to use — and why a masked human genome matters — is covered in Decontamination.

docs.title: 4. Adapter and quality trimming
docs.text:
Rule trim_adapters, always runs.

fastp removes adapter read-through, trims poor quality from both ends with a sliding window (--cut_front --cut_right), and drops reads that end up shorter than shotgun.fastp.min_read_length (default 100; around 70 suits HiSeq 2×100 data). Adapters are detected from the data itself (--detect_adapter_for_pe), so no adapter file is needed.

Input: whichever decontaminated stage ran last, or the raw reads if both are off. Output: {sample}_trim_R1/_R2.fastq.gz (temporary) and the {sample}_fastp.html / {sample}_fastp.json reports. The JSON is used three times over: by MultiQC, by the read tracking table, and by Bracken, which reads the post-trim mean read length out of it.

docs.title: 5. Kraken2 classification
docs.text:
Rule kraken2.

Kraken2 walks each read pair k-mer by k-mer, looking up the minimizer of each k-mer in the database — every k-mer sharing a minimizer inherits that minimizer's stored lowest common ancestor, which is why one database entry can account for a whole run of apparent k-mer hits. The taxa hit form a small tree, each node weighted by how many hits it received, and the read is labelled with the leaf of the highest-scoring root-to-leaf path (the LCA of the leaves if two paths tie). A handful of stray hits to a distant taxon therefore does not drag the whole read up the taxonomy.

shotgun:
  kraken:
    confidence: 0.15      # higher = stricter
    hit_groups: 3         # minimum distinct hit groups per read
    memory_mapping: true
    threads: null         # null = use resources.threads.kraken2

confidence is the fraction of a read's k-mers that must fall inside the clade of the taxon the read is assigned to. A read that falls short is not simply rejected: Kraken2 moves the label up the taxonomy until the score clears the threshold, and calls the read unclassified only when not even root qualifies. Raising it therefore mostly pushes assignments to coarser ranks — which leaves more work for Bracken in step 6 — and only secondarily increases the unclassified fraction. A sweep from 0.00 to 1.00 on simulated samples (Wright et al. 2023) found the best setting depends on what is being optimised: 0.60 gave the highest mean F1, while 0.15 gave the lowest L1 distance and the best recall and precision over the reads actually classified. MetaFlux defaults to 0.15, which favours accurate relative abundances; 0.15 is also the threshold used for CAMI2 benchmarking by Nyström-Persson et al. (2025).

hit_groups counts hit groups, not k-mer hits. A hit group is a run of overlapping k-mers that share one minimizer found in the database — one lookup, at one place in the read — so a read can show dozens of k-mer hits and still amount to a single group. hit_groups: 3 requires three such separate hits before a classification stands (Kraken2's own default is 2), leaving a read unclassified when all its evidence sits at one locus.

Input: the fastp-trimmed reads and the Kraken2 database. Output, in 02.classification/kraken2/:

File Contents {sample}_report.txt the per-taxon summary tree, written with --report-minimizer-data {sample}_output.txt one line per read pair with its assignment {sample}_R1.fastq.gz / _R2.fastq.gz the reads Kraken2 could classify

The classified-read FASTQs are kept, not deleted, because per-taxon read extraction draws from them. The report is consumed by Bracken, by MultiQC and by read extraction, which finds the taxon and everything below it there; the per-read output is consumed by read extraction.

The report format is not the standard one

--report-minimizer-data adds two columns to the usual Kraken2 report, which shifts the rank and taxid columns. KrakenTools reads the report as it stands, but anything else parsing these reports needs to account for the shift.

Memory behaviour is the main practical concern here and is covered in Reference databases.

docs.title: 6. Bracken abundance re-estimation
docs.text:
Rule bracken.

Kraken2 leaves many reads assigned above species level, at whatever ancestor the k-mers agreed on. Bracken pushes those reads back down using the database's k-mer distributions, giving abundances at a chosen rank.

shotgun:
  bracken:
    tax_lev: S            # P | C | O | F | G | S (D and K are refused)
    threshold: auto       # auto = scaled to each sample's depth; or a fixed read count

Bracken's estimates depend on read length, and the database ships pre-computed distributions for several lengths (50, 75, 100, 150, 200, 250 and 300 bp). MetaFlux reads the mean post-trim read length from the sample's fastp JSON and picks the closest available distribution automatically — using a 150 bp distribution on 100 bp reads would bias the redistribution. With threshold: auto the minimum read count is computed from the sample's classified read pairs in the same step. All three small calculations (mean length, closest distribution, threshold) are done with jq from the Bracken environment, so they give the same answer on any machine.

MetaFlux pins Bracken 3.1p1, bioconda's build of 3.1 with a fix for the report: with tax_lev other than S, plain 3.1 writes 0 reads assigned directly to a taxon (third column of {sample}_report.txt) on almost every row. The abundances MetaFlux reports come from the clade counts and are the same with either build.

Input: the Kraken2 report plus the fastp JSON. Output, in 03.abundance/: {sample}_report.txt (Bracken's re-estimated report) and {sample}_output.txt (the per-taxon abundance table). The reports are consumed by the OTU-table step and by MultiQC.

Drop to genus on a shallow database

Species-level re-estimation is only as good as the database's species representation. With a small or size-capped index, tax_lev: G gives a more reliable table. The OTU table then lists genera, one row each, with an empty species slot.

The numbers in the OTU table are estimates, and they do not sum to the classified reads

Two things about Bracken's output are easy to misread, and both matter when the numbers reach a methods section or a normalisation step.

They are estimated, not observed. A value in otu_table.tsv is not a count of reads that Kraken2 assigned to that taxon. It is Bracken's estimate of how many reads originated from it, after redistributing reads that Kraken2 had left at coarser ranks. Reporting Bracken's estimates as observed assignments overstates what was measured.

They do not account for every classified read. Bracken reports only at the target rank. Reads classified above it that cannot be pushed down — because the evidence does not separate the descendants — are absent from the output altogether. So the column total of otu_table.tsv is smaller than the classified column in stats/read_tracking.txt, and the two are not meant to reconcile. When a relative abundance is computed, be explicit about which denominator was used: the OTU-table total, or the classified reads.

docs.title: 7. OTU table
docs.text:
Rule finalize_otu_table.

MetaFlux builds the OTU table itself, straight from the per-sample Bracken reports: one row per taxon at shotgun.bracken.tax_lev, one column per sample, and in each cell Bracken's re-estimated read count for that taxon (the clade count of its row in the sample's report). Taxa appear in the order they are first met, reading the samples in the order of the table's columns, which are sorted by sample name (as in samples.tsv).

Every row carries a lineage of eight fixed slots, one for each rank code Kraken2 prints in its reports, on any database:

d__ k__ p__ c__ o__ f__ g__ s__      domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
  • Where the names come from. A slot takes the name of the row, on the path from the report's root down to the taxon, whose code is exactly the slot's letter (D, K, P …). Rows with a numbered code (K1, P3, R2 …) are in-between nodes and get no slot, with one exception: a virus realm, which Kraken2 also prints with a numbered code (R2; D1 on a database built when NCBI still ranked Viruses a superkingdom), fills d__ (below).
  • Empty slots. A rank that the lineage does not have leaves its slot empty: k__ is empty in every row on a GTDB database, which has no kingdom rank, and on NCBI databases for the taxa NCBI places in no kingdom, most protists among them; at tax_lev: G the s__ slot is empty.
  • Viruses carry their realm in d__. A virus has no domain. Its d__ slot holds its realm, the top rank of virus taxonomy, and its viral kingdom sits in k__, on every NCBI database. Kraken2 has no rank code for a realm, so MetaFlux recognises realms by their rank in the database's own taxonomy file, taxo.k2d (see Reference databases). A virus without a realm keeps an empty d__, as do plasmids. Viruses itself is never written as a domain, also on a database built when NCBI still ranked it a superkingdom.
  • Species names are whole, exactly as the database writes them.
d__Bacteria;k__Pseudomonadati;p__Pseudomonadota;c__Gammaproteobacteria;o__Enterobacterales;f__Enterobacteriaceae;g__Escherichia;s__Escherichia coli
d__Eukaryota;k__Fungi;p__Ascomycota;c__Pichiomycetes;o__Serinales;f__Debaryomycetaceae;g__Candida;s__Candida albicans
d__Duplodnaviria;k__Heunggongvirae;p__Uroviricota;c__Caudoviricetes;o__;f__Peduoviridae;g__Peduovirus;s__Peduovirus P37

While it builds the table, the step also checks the reports and stops on two things it cannot trust: a D or K code that disagrees with the database (reports written by a Kraken2 older than 2.17, which codes NCBI's domains R1 or R2, or reports made with another database), and one taxon with two different lineages. See Troubleshooting.

Then it applies the optional taxon filter:

shotgun:
  taxonomy_filter:
    enabled: false
    keep:    []           # e.g. [d__Bacteria, d__Archaea]
    discard: []           # e.g. [g__Homo]

The filter uses the same rank-aware token matching as the amplicon side — each token must match a whole segment of the lineage, never a loose substring — and it runs on the final table only, after Bracken. It therefore changes which OTUs appear in the table, never how a read was classified. It is off by default because metagenomic sample types vary too much for a sensible universal setting. Common uses are keeping prokaryotes (keep: [d__Bacteria, d__Archaea], which drops viruses too, since their d__ slot holds a realm) and dropping residual host (discard: [g__Homo]). The tokens are checked against the eight slots and the Kraken2 database when the run starts, so a token that can never match (k__Bacteria, now d__Bacteria) stops the run before Kraken2 does any work. If the filter would remove every taxon, the step stops with an error that names the tokens and lists the d__ values in the table, rather than writing an empty table. The machinery is described in full under Keeping and discarding taxa.

Output: 03.abundance/otu_table.biom and 03.abundance/otu_table.tsv, written from the same rows and numbers, so they always agree. These are the main deliverable of a shotgun run. With profiler: both the sylph table next to them has seven slots and no k__, so compare the two by rank name (see taxonomy strings in the final tables).

docs.title: 8. Per-taxon read extraction (optional)
docs.text:
Rules extract_taxon_reads and compress_extracted — only run when shotgun.extract_taxa is non-empty.

KrakenTools pulls the reads assigned to a named taxon, and everything below it, into per-sample FASTQ files — the starting point for a targeted assembly or a closer look at one organism. See Per-taxon read extraction.

docs.title: What lands on disk
docs.text:
out_dir/
├── 01.preprocessing/     # dephix / dehost stats, fastp JSON + HTML, host index
├── 02.classification/
│   ├── kraken2/          # Kraken2 reports, per-read output, classified reads, k-mer evidence
│   └── sylph/            # sylph sketches and sylph-tax files (profiler sylph | both)
├── 03.abundance/         # Bracken reports, otu_table.tsv / otu_table.biom
├── 04.extracted_reads/   # KrakenTools per-taxon reads (only if extract_taxa set)
├── stats/                # read_tracking.txt
├── multiqc/              # multiqc_report.html
├── samples.tsv           # sample → source → FASTQ manifest
└── logs/                 # per-rule logs

The cleaned reads themselves are marked temporary: Snakemake deletes the _dephix, _dehost and _trim FASTQs as soon as the rule that needed them has finished, so 01.preprocessing/ keeps QC and statistics rather than several copies of the library. What stays there is:

File Present when {sample}_fastp.html / _fastp.json always {sample}_dephix_stats.txt remove_phix: true {sample}_dehost_stats.txt host_genomes is set refs/bbmap_index/ (BBMap host index) host_genomes is set

The concatenated host reference, refs/host_combined.fna.gz, is temporary as well: it is deleted once the index has been built, which is why a URL in host_genomes is fetched again on every fresh run.

Read stats/read_tracking.txt first after a run. One row per sample, counts in read pairs throughout, columns in pipeline order:

sample → raw → [nophix] → [no_host] → trimmed → classified → unclassified

The bracketed columns appear only when the corresponding step ran. A large drop at no_host means the sample was host-dominated — but only when PhiX removal ran too. With remove_phix: false the raw column is taken from the fastp report, that is, from the reads entering fastp, which is the output of host removal; raw and no_host then count exactly the same reads and no host drop can appear however host-dominated the sample is. In that configuration read the mapping rate out of logs/decontam_host/{sample}.log instead.

A large unclassified fraction usually points at the database rather than the data — an environment poorly covered by the chosen index, not a failed run.

multiqc/multiqc_report.html collects the fastp, Kraken2, Bracken and BBTools statistics into one page.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Reference databases — picking a Kraken2 index and keeping its memory use under control.
  • Decontamination — PhiX and host removal in detail.
  • Per-taxon read extraction — pulling reads for one taxon.

docs.title: Per-taxon read extraction
docs.text:
A classification table says which organisms are present and in what proportion. It does not give the reads back. When the next question is about sequence rather than abundance — assemble the Pseudomonas fraction, look for a resistance gene in the Escherichia coli reads, hand the eukaryotic fraction to a different tool — the reads belonging to one taxon have to be pulled out of the library.

That is what this optional step does, using KrakenTools. It is off unless taxa are named:

Extracted read counts will not match the OTU table

The two numbers answer different questions and are expected to differ, usually with fewer reads extracted than the OTU table suggests. Extraction returns the reads Kraken2 actually assigned to that clade. The OTU table holds Bracken's estimates after redistributing reads from coarser ranks — an estimate of origin, not a set of reads that can be handed back. A taxon credited with 50,000 reads in otu_table.tsv may yield considerably fewer here, and neither figure is wrong.

shotgun:
  extract_taxa: []          # empty = skip extraction entirely

shotgun:
  extract_taxa: [Bacteria, Escherichia coli]

With an empty list the extraction rules are never added to the run, so nothing is computed and no 04.extracted_reads/ directory appears.

docs.title: Naming taxa
docs.text:
Entries are NCBI scientific names, written as they appear in the classification report — Bacteria, Fungi, Pseudomonas, Escherichia coli.

The name is matched at whatever rank it occurs in the report. There is no rank setting and no restriction: a domain, a phylum, a genus and a single species are all named the same way and handled identically. Reads assigned to the named taxon and to everything below it are extracted, so Bacteria yields the bacterial fraction of the sample and Escherichia coli that one species, its strains included.

Both the lookup and the walk down the tree (--include-children) use the sample's own Kraken2 report, 02.classification/kraken2/{sample}_report.txt. It lists every taxon that Kraken2 assigned at least one read to, strains and other ranks below species included, so the read pairs extracted for a taxon are exactly its clade count in that report (the second column). The Bracken settings (tax_lev, threshold) and the k-mer evidence gate do not change this report, so they do not change which reads are extracted.

Up to v2.4.0 MetaFlux used the Bracken report here, which has no rows below tax_lev and none for the taxa Bracken dropped below its threshold. The reads Kraken2 had placed on those rows were left out, without a warning: for a species whose genomes sit under a strain taxid, often all of them. In the ZymoBIOMICS Gut Microbiome Standard (D6331), SRA run SRR38976715 (BioProject PRJNA1474435; see Benchmark data), Kraken2 with PlusPF k2_pluspf_20260626 placed all 29,618 Candida albicans read pairs on the strain SC5314 and none on the species itself. An extraction based on the Bracken report would have found none of them.

The name must match one report row exactly

The taxid is found by looking for the row of the sample's Kraken2 report whose name, without the indentation that shows its place in the tree, is exactly the name given, capital letters included. A partial name therefore finds nothing: coli does not match Escherichia coli, and Prevotella finds the genus, not the family Prevotellaceae listed above it. Write the full scientific name.

Some names occur in more than one row of a report. A genus and a subgenus of the same name, such as Plasmodium and Leishmania, are resolved: the subgenus row (rank code G1) lies inside the genus row (G), so MetaFlux extracts the genus, whose reads include those of the subgenus, and writes a note in the log. The rule is narrow: exactly one of the rows has a plain rank code, and every other row has that letter with a number and lies inside it. In any other case, such as a placeholder name that GTDB gives to an order, a family and a genus alike, or two taxa that share a name, MetaFlux cannot tell which of them is meant, so the run stops with a message that lists the rows, with their rank codes and taxids. Remove the name from extract_taxa, and extract the taxon you mean by hand with KrakenTools (the bioconda package krakentools), giving it the taxid from the message:

extract_kraken_reads.py -t <taxid> --include-children \
    -k 02.classification/kraken2/<sample>_output.txt \
    -r 02.classification/kraken2/<sample>_report.txt \
    -1 02.classification/kraken2/<sample>_R1.fastq.gz \
    -2 02.classification/kraken2/<sample>_R2.fastq.gz \
    --fastq-output -o <taxon>_R1.fastq -o2 <taxon>_R2.fastq

KrakenTools reads the report as it is. Anything else that picks fields out of it by position must allow for the two columns that --report-minimizer-data adds: the taxid and the name sit in fields 7 and 8, not in the usual 5 and 6.

A single species gives an approximate read set

Kraken2 assigns each read on its own, from the k-mers it shares with the genomes in the database, so the reads extracted for one species are not exactly that species' reads:

  • reads of close relatives get mixed in, above all of relatives the database lacks: their reads land on the nearest species it holds;
  • part of the species' own reads are missing, often most of them. Kraken2 places a read that matches several taxa on the lowest node they share, and extraction takes only the reads placed on the named taxon or below it. Escherichia coli reads that also match Shigella, a separate genus in NCBI's taxonomy, are placed on the family Enterobacteriaceae. There can be many times more of them there than on E. coli itself (about 30 times more in the D6331 run SRR38976715), while Bracken's estimate in the OTU table gives them back to E. coli.

To collect reads for an assembly or a gene search, name the lowest rank that holds them: often the genus, but for E. coli, whose reads shared with Shigella sit on the family, Enterobacteriaceae, which also brings in the reads of its other genera. The direct-read column of 02.classification/kraken2/{sample}_report.txt (the third) shows on which rows Kraken2 placed them. Use a species-level extraction to check a doubtful species call instead: map the extracted reads to a genome of that species and look at how evenly they cover it. Reads spread over the whole genome support the call; reads piled up on a few regions, such as conserved genes or mobile elements, point to a relative or to a false positive. Either way it is a check, not proof.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
For each sample and each named taxon:

  1. The taxon's NCBI taxid is looked up in that sample's Kraken2 report (02.classification/kraken2/{sample}_report.txt): the row whose name is exactly the requested name. The lookup runs with the Python of the KrakenTools environment, so it does not depend on the tools installed on the host.
  2. extract_kraken_reads.py reads the Kraken2 per-read output (02.classification/kraken2/{sample}_output.txt), which records the assignment of every read pair, together with the same Kraken2 report so it can walk the taxonomy below the target taxid (--include-children).
  3. The matching read pairs are written out as FASTQ and then compressed with pigz — extract_kraken_reads.py cannot write gzip itself, so a separate rule does it.

The reads come from the classified-read FASTQs Kraken2 wrote (02.classification/kraken2/{sample}_R1.fastq.gz and _R2.fastq.gz), which is why those files are kept rather than deleted. Reads Kraken2 could not classify are not in that pool and can never be extracted — extraction only ever pulls out reads that already carry a Kraken2 assignment.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
out_dir/04.extracted_reads/
├── {sample}_bacteria_R1.fastq.gz
├── {sample}_bacteria_R2.fastq.gz
├── {sample}_escherichia_coli_R1.fastq.gz
└── {sample}_escherichia_coli_R2.fastq.gz

The taxon part of the filename is the configured name lowercased with spaces replaced by underscores, so Escherichia coli becomes escherichia_coli. Pairing is preserved: R1 and R2 stay in step and can go straight into an assembler or a mapper.

One pair of files is produced per sample per taxon, so three taxa across forty samples is 240 files. Naming a broad group such as Bacteria in a host-depleted metagenome writes most of the classified reads out a second time, so check the free disk space first.

docs.title: When a taxon is absent
docs.text:
If no row in a sample's Kraken2 report matches the name, the rule writes empty FASTQ files and records the reason in logs/extract_taxon_reads/{sample}_{taxon}.log:

no taxid found for 'Escherichia coli'

Empty output is deliberate: Snakemake needs the declared files to exist for the run to finish, and an absent taxon in one sample should not fail the whole workflow. An unexpectedly empty file is a signal to check the log — either Kraken2 assigned no read of that sample to the taxon, or the name did not match anything in the report.

The OTU table does not decide what can be extracted. A taxon that Bracken dropped for falling below shotgun.bracken.threshold (see Reference databases) has no row in otu_table.tsv, but its reads are in Kraken2's report, and they are extracted.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
Rule threads mem_mb What it does extract_taxon_reads 4 2000 taxid lookup + read extraction compress_extracted 6 (not declared) pigz compression of the extracted FASTQs

The uncompressed intermediates are marked temporary and are removed once compressed, so only the .fastq.gz files remain.

docs.title: sylph, the alternative profiler
docs.text:
sylph is a second way to turn the cleaned shotgun reads into a taxon table. It runs instead of Kraken2 + Bracken, or next to them, when shotgun.profiler asks for it. The cleaning in front (PhiX removal, host removal, fastp) is the same whichever profiler runs.

Kraken2 + Bracken stays the default

sylph is available from v2.5.0 and is used only when shotgun.profiler is set to sylph or both. With the default, kraken2, nothing on this page applies.

docs.title: What sylph does differently
docs.text:
• It compares sketches, not reads. sylph reduces each sample to a sketch, a fixed subset of about one in 200 of its 31-bp k-mers, and compares it with sketches of whole reference genomes.
  • It reports genomes, at about species level. A genome is reported when the sample holds something at 95 % average nucleotide identity (ANI) or more to it, roughly the species boundary. Each row of the table is one reference genome.
  • Abundance comes from coverage. From how many of a genome's k-mers turn up, and how often, sylph estimates how deeply the genome is covered. Multiplying that coverage by the genome's length gives the amount of sequence the genome contributed to the sample, and from that its share of the reads.
  • No read gets a label. sylph writes no per-read output, so read extraction, which picks reads by the taxon Kraken2 gave each one, has nothing to work from. The k-mer evidence gate needs Kraken2 too: it filters the Kraken2 report before Bracken, and under sylph neither runs.
  • Same reads as Kraken2. sylph sketches exactly the trimmed read pairs Kraken2 would classify. With profiler: both the two tables come from identical input; they are written side by side and never merged.

docs.title: Switching it on
docs.text:
shotgun:
  profiler: sylph              # kraken2 (default) | sylph | both

references:
  sylph_databases:
    - path: /db/sylph/gtdb-r232-c200-dbv1.syldb
      taxonomy: GTDB_r232
    - path: /db/sylph/fungi-refseq-2025-10-11-c200-dbv1.syldb
      taxonomy: FungiRefSeq-latest
  sylph_taxonomy_dir: /db/sylph_taxonomy

With sylph, the Kraken2 database is not needed and references.kraken_db can keep its placeholder. With both, Kraken2 + Bracken and sylph run on the same reads in one run, and fastp still runs once per sample.

All databases are profiled in one sylph run, so within a sample an organism present in two of them is reported once, by its closer genome.

Everything in the block above is checked before the first job starts: the file names, a taxonomy for every database and the lineage table behind each. When a database file name shows its release (gtdb-r232-c200-dbv1.syldb, or a copy renamed gtdb_r232_c200.syldb), MetaFlux also checks that the taxonomy comes from the same release. That covers a built-in name and a lineage table given by its path under a built-in table's file name (gtdb_r226_metadata.tsv.gz, say); a table of your own under another name cannot be matched to a release at this point. After profiling, MetaFlux checks the GTDB release once more, from the genome paths in sylph's output, whatever the files are called. A mistake stops the run with a message that says what to change.

docs.title: Databases and lineage tables, set up once
docs.text:
MetaFlux does not download sylph databases, just as it does not download a Kraken2 index. The pre-built ones are listed on sylph's Pre-built databases page.

  • Sketch density. MetaFlux sketches the reads at c 200, and a database must be built at the same density or a coarser one. c 200 builds find low-coverage genomes best; c 1000 builds need about a fifth of the memory. A c 100 build would make sylph skip every sample, so MetaFlux stops on it.
  • File types. Both .syldb and the two-stage .syl2db files work.
  • One database per family. Two GTDB releases, or the c 200 and c 1000 builds of one release, share genomes and names, and listing both stops the run.
  • GTDB or GlobDB, not both. GlobDB already holds every genome of the GTDB database, with the same lineage, under its accession without the version suffix (GCF_003096595 for GTDB's GCF_003096595.1), and adds genomes from MAG catalogues. Listed together, each GTDB genome would be loaded twice. sylph would report it from one copy or the other, and which one can change from sample to sample, so one genome could end up on two rows, each with zeros where the other copy was reported: genome-level counts, prevalence and diversity would be wrong. The pair would also need more memory without adding a species, about 26 GB more with GTDB r232 at c 200. MetaFlux therefore stops before the first job when both are listed, whether their taxonomies are given by name or by path. List GlobDB alone (it covers GTDB) or GTDB alone; a fungal database such as FungiRefSeq can go next to either.
  • No viral databases. IMG/VR and UHGV use viral ranks that do not fit the table and are refused.

Each database is paired with the sylph-tax taxonomy that names its genomes:

Database file taxonomy: gtdb-r232-c200-dbv1.syldb or gtdb-r232-c1000-dbv1.syldb GTDB_r232 gtdb-r226-c200-dbv1.syldb or gtdb-r226-c1000-dbv1.syldb GTDB_r226 globdb_r232_sylph_c200.syldb GlobDB_r232 fungi-refseq-2025-10-11-c200-dbv1.syldb FungiRefSeq-latest a database you built the path of your own accession<TAB>lineage table (.tsv or .tsv.gz)

For the GlobDB file, sylph's Pre-built databases page sends you to the GlobDB website: globdb_r232_sylph_c200.syldb is on GlobDB's own download server, in the release's taxonomic_profiling/ folder, next to GlobDB's copy of the lineage table.

The built-in taxonomies read their lineage tables from references.sylph_taxonomy_dir. Fill that folder once, with the sylph-tax version MetaFlux pins in workflow/envs/sylph.yaml (sylph 1.0.0, sylph-tax 1.9.2):

conda env create -n metaflux-sylph -f workflow/envs/sylph.yaml
conda run -n metaflux-sylph sylph-tax --no-config --taxonomy-dir /db/sylph_taxonomy download

This fetches every table sylph-tax knows, about 80 MB, from Zenodo and, for GlobDB r232, from the GlobDB server. One failed download stops the whole command. The tables can also be fetched one at a time, for example the two used above:

wget -P /db/sylph_taxonomy https://zenodo.org/records/19646381/files/gtdb_r232_metadata.tsv.gz
wget -P /db/sylph_taxonomy https://zenodo.org/records/17330476/files/fungi_refseq_2025-10-11_metadata.tsv.gz

MetaFlux always calls sylph-tax with --no-config --taxonomy-dir, so nothing is read from or written to ~/.config/sylph-tax.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
File What it holds 03.abundance/sylph_table.tsv the main table: estimated read pairs per genome and sample, and a last row unassigned 03.abundance/sylph_table.biom the same table in BIOM (HDF5) format 03.abundance/sylph_table.genome_copies.tsv each genome's share of genome copies (%) among the detected genomes; same rows, no unassigned 03.abundance/sylph_genomes.tsv one row per genome: species name, whether it is a placeholder, the FASTA header of the reference genome, the placeholder-genus flag, best coverage and ANI 03.abundance/sylph_profile.tsv sylph's own output, unchanged: one row per sample and genome stats/sylph/sylph_summary.tsv one row per sample: read pairs after QC, how much of them the detected genomes explain, genomes found, flagged genomes

stats/read_tracking.txt is written as in every shotgun run; under profiler: sylph it has no Kraken2 columns and ends with trimmed. The MultiQC report gets a table section for sylph. 02.classification/sylph/ keeps the sketches, so a later run in the same folder with other databases does not sketch again.

In sylph_table.tsv, line 1 is a comment that says what the numbers are and which databases they come from, and line 2 is the header, with #OTU ID, the samples and taxonomy. Each row ID is a genome accession, and the lineage has seven slots, the GTDB ranks from domain to species:

#OTU ID sampleA sampleB taxonomy
GCF_000146045.2_R64 1520    0   d__Eukaryota;p__Ascomycota;c__Saccharomycetes;o__Saccharomycetales;f__Saccharomycetaceae;g__Saccharomyces;s__Saccharomyces cerevisiae
unassigned  0   98211   d__Unassigned;p__;c__;o__;f__;g__;s__

The first slot always holds the domain and is always written d__: d__Bacteria, d__Archaea or d__Eukaryota, and d__Unassigned on the unassigned row. GTDB has no kingdom rank, so there is no k__ slot. The FungiRefSeq-latest lineage table writes its domain as k__Eukaryota, and the TaraEukaryoticSMAG table spells it Eukarya in some rows; MetaFlux writes both as d__Eukaryota, so every row uses the same seven prefixes. A lineage whose first rank is not a domain stops the run with a message that names the lineage table. The lineage of the Kraken2 table is described on the output files page.

With profiler: both the two tables do not line up column by column. otu_table.tsv has eight slots on any Kraken2 database, d__ k__ p__ c__ o__ f__ g__ s__, and this table seven, without k__; and the two databases can name the same organism differently. Methanobrevibacter smithii in the D6331 run SRR38976715 (BioProject PRJNA1474435; see Benchmark data), as Kraken2 names it with PlusPF k2_pluspf_20260626 (above) and as sylph names it with GTDB r232 (below):

d__Archaea;k__Methanobacteriati;p__Methanobacteriota;c__Methanobacteria;o__Methanobacteriales;f__Methanobacteriaceae;g__Methanobrevibacter;s__Methanobrevibacter smithii
d__Archaea;p__Methanobacteriota;c__Methanobacteria;o__Methanobacteriales;f__Methanobacteriaceae;g__Methanocatella;s__Methanocatella smithii

No MetaFlux step joins the two tables. Compare them by rank name, not by column position.

docs.title: Reading the numbers
docs.text:
• Estimated read pairs, not counted ones. A value in sylph_table.tsv is sylph's Sequence_abundance, the share of the sample's reads that genome explains, estimated from its coverage, times the sample's read pairs after QC, rounded to a whole pair. No read was assigned to the genome. Each column adds up to the trimmed count of stats/read_tracking.txt, except by a few pairs per million in a sample sylph explains to 100 % (explained_capped: yes). There the rounded genome rows can add up to slightly more than trimmed (unassigned is then 0, and logs/sylph_tables.log says so), or leave a few pairs over in unassigned.
  • unassigned is a model estimate as well. MetaFlux runs sylph profile -u, which estimates how much of each sample the detected genomes do not explain; that remainder is the unassigned row. It depends on the database, since a fuller database explains more. unassigned cannot be compared with Kraken2's unclassified read pairs. Leave the row out before computing relative abundances of the detected genomes.
  • Read accuracy. The estimates also depend on sylph's estimate of read accuracy. When the sample's genomes are covered too thinly for that estimate (common in shallow samples, and in very diverse ones even when deeply sequenced: it happened in all ten simulated CAMI II marine samples), sylph assumes 99.5 % instead; read_accuracy in the summary then reads fixed 99.5% (high diversity for the depth), after sylph's own words for this case (high diversity compared to sequencing depth). That assumption moves every genome row of the sample by one common factor, and the unassigned row with them; which genomes are found, and their genome copies, do not change. On the four metagenomes of BioProject PRJNA1477390 (runs SRR39106521–SRR39106524; see Shotgun test dataset), where sylph's own estimate was about 99.9 %, forcing 99.5 % raised the explained share by 12–14 % of its value (3 to 8 percentage points). Compare explained shares, unassigned and estimated pairs only between samples with the same read_accuracy. Otherwise leave out unassigned and compare shares among the detected genomes, or use sylph_table.genome_copies.tsv.
  • Capped samples. explained_capped: yes usually means that sylph's coverage estimates added up to at least all of the sample's sequence (sylph does not report the uncapped sum). sylph then shares 100 % among the detected genomes, as it does without -u, so every genome's estimated read pairs in that sample are scaled down by that unknown amount, and they change when a database is added or removed, even for a genome whose coverage stays the same. Nothing is left for unassigned to estimate. Compare a capped sample with others by shares among the detected genomes or by genome copies, not by estimated pairs.
  • Genome copies are a different share. sylph_table.genome_copies.tsv gives each genome's share of genome copies, roughly of cells, among the detected genomes only. A genome that is large but present in few copies has a high read share and a low copy share.
  • Names are kept as GTDB writes them. That includes placeholder species such as s__JABGUH01 sp018646675, genera and species split with a suffix (g__Blautia_A; s__Escherichia coli_E is a real, named species), and GTDB's own genus names (s__Methanocatella smithii for the species long known as Methanobrevibacter smithii). Comparisons at genus level are less affected than at species level. The name_status column of sylph_genomes.tsv says for every genome whether its name is a placeholder.

docs.title: The placeholder-genus flag
docs.text: GTDB sometimes puts a genome in a genus known only by a code (a placeholder genus such as g__G047199095) while the genome's own FASTA header, written by whoever submitted it, names a Latin species of another genus. In GTDB r232 this is the case for some Escherichia coli assemblies that are new in that release: reads of an E. coli strain can land on such a genome, so that the strain appears under a placeholder name and not as Escherichia coli. MetaFlux renames and merges nothing. It flags the genome in sylph_genomes.tsv (GTDB placeholder genus; genome labelled Escherichia coli) and counts the flagged genomes of each sample in the summary. In the D6331 run SRR38976715 it flagged two, GCA_047199095.1 and GCA_047199115.1.

docs.title: Reading the tables
docs.text:
The first line of each table is a comment, so skip it:

tab <- read.delim("03.abundance/sylph_table.tsv", skip = 1, row.names = 1,
                  check.names = FALSE, comment.char = "")

import pandas as pd
tab = pd.read_csv("03.abundance/sylph_table.tsv", sep="\t", skiprows=1, index_col=0)

Do not pass comment="#" to pandas: the header line itself starts with #OTU ID.

phyloseq reads the BIOM file. Its parse_taxonomy_greengenes knows the prefixes k__ to s__ but not d__, so the first column comes out named Rank1; rename it:

library(phyloseq)
ps <- import_biom("03.abundance/sylph_table.biom",
                  parseFunction = parse_taxonomy_greengenes)
colnames(tax_table(ps))[1] <- "Domain"

docs.title: Settings that do not apply
docs.text: Under profiler: sylph, shotgun.extract_taxa (it needs Kraken2's per-read output) and shotgun.kmer_evidence (it filters the Kraken2 report before Bracken) are switched off with a warning; under both they still act on the Kraken2 side. shotgun.taxonomy_filter and the shotgun.kraken and shotgun.bracken settings act on the Kraken2 chain only. The sylph tables are written unfiltered, so each column still adds up to the read pairs after QC (with the one exception under Reading the numbers).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Sample names must not look like numbers. sylph-tax reads sample names with pandas, which turns 001 into 1, merges 01 with 1 and drops NA. MetaFlux stops at start-up on such names; rename the files so that each name contains a letter (S001). Names such as 12_3 are fine.
  • A sample with no read pairs left after QC stops the run, because sylph cannot sketch an empty file. Remove it from fastq_dir, or profile it with Kraken2.
  • Adding sylph to a finished Kraken2 run needs a new out_dir, with profiler: sylph. The trimmed reads of the finished run were deleted after use, so both in the same folder would make them again and run Kraken2 again. MetaFlux stops and says so.
  • Lineages must start with a domain. Among the built-in taxonomies, only GlobDB r226 has genomes without one: 754 of them have Unclassified as their first rank (d__Unclassified). MetaFlux therefore refuses GlobDB r226 at start-up: its taxonomy (GlobDB_r226, or its lineage table given by its path), and any database whose file name says GlobDB r226 (globdb_r226_…), whatever taxonomy it is paired with. Use GlobDB r232 instead, the database globdb_r232_sylph_c200.syldb with taxonomy: GlobDB_r232, which places every genome in a domain. A lineage table of your own whose first rank is not a domain stops the run at sylph_tables, once sylph detects one of its genomes.
  • Memory. sylph holds every database in memory, in a single sylph_profile job for all samples. MetaFlux asks for 1.2 times the size of the database files plus 4 GB; set resources.mem_mb.sylph_profile to a number to override it, for example on a cluster, but keep it above about 1.1 times the size of the files, plus some headroom. GTDB r232 at c 200 with the fungal database is about 27 GB of files. With a few samples, most of the job's time goes into reading the databases from disk. Do not size the job from benchmarks/sylph_profile.tsv: sylph's memory climbs while it reads the databases and peaks only in the last seconds of the job, and after its first 30 checks (about the first 15 to 20 seconds) Snakemake records memory only every 30 seconds, so the recorded max_rss usually misses the peak and can be far below it.
  • Memory under both. The sylph_profile job can start while Kraken2 jobs are running. On a local run, Snakemake keeps their memory apart only when it is given a cap, with --resources mem_mb=.... Give a cap at least as large as the sylph_profile figure printed at start-up plus what the Kraken2 jobs declare. A smaller cap does not stop the run: Snakemake lowers the job's request to the cap and runs it anyway.
  • Reproducibility. Sketches are made with one thread (resources.threads.sylph_sketch: 1), because with more threads they differ slightly from run to run; with one thread they are the same every time, also with PhiX or host removal on. The thread count of sylph_profile changes no number. Genomes with exactly the same abundance, common in mock communities, can come out in a different order from run to run in sylph_profile.tsv and in sylph-tax's files, so sort those before comparing two runs; the MetaFlux tables sort their own rows. Each sketch records the path of the reads it was made from, so sketches of the same reads in two out_dirs are not byte-identical.
